The last ten years have been marked by significant breakthroughs in neutrino physics. Notably, multiple studies have conclusively proven the occurrence of neutrino flavor oscillations. We have established the parameters for neutrino mixing, which allows us to design more effective investigations of newly opened avenues of research. One such area of study is the path towards a more comprehensive understanding of three-neutrino physics, particularly on the topic of whether the parameters allow for CP violation. Another area of focus lies on the development of more precise geoneutrino detection methods, which can provide valuable insights into the composition and structure of the Earth. Moreover, we are on the verge of breaking new ground in particle physics with the deployment of the first reactor neutrino experiment capable of probing the possibility of physics beyond the Standard Model.

Research on top tagging has advanced rapidly due to the top quark's substantial role in studying physics that goes beyond the standard model. Recent studies have found that machine learning techniques have improved tagging and classification capabilities for top jets compared to previous methods. These advancements have primarily focused on the study of the interactions of the Higgs boson and top quarks. This work uses the $t\bar{t}Z$ production mode at hadron colliders to test the ability of observe and study heavy resonances with spin greater than one, such as the Dorvall and Fajans-Soper unitarization methods predict. These models generate anomalous distributions in the kinematic properties of the Z boson, allowing for the development of machine learning strategies to identify signal events. Next, the work examines whether the top quark can be used as a probe to study the nature of neutrino masses. Using the concept of top tagging as a novel method for identifying collective neutrino masses through charged lepton jet reconstruction, this work proposes a new tagging variable to improve research in this area.

This document establishes the fundamental elements for virtual organizations, requirement refinement, abstractions of models, and concrete instantiations. The document also examines Virtual Organizations within these contexts.

To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts sample efficiency, particularly in challenging multi-variable environments and high-dimensional sensory spaces.

Two new strategies have been proposed to apply the supersymmetry method from Gaussian matrices to broader rotation-invariant matrices. Specifically, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization formula have emerged as viable approaches. By showing the equivalence of these strategies, we aim to demonstrate their common effectiveness, ultimately involving the transformation of supersymmetric matrix integrals into related quadratic supermatrix calculations with defined symmetry constraints.

This paper addresses challenges in spatiotemporal predictive learning approaches, including short-term and long-term forecasting issues. A novel framework called spatiotemporal predictive learning (ST-PL) is introduced, which centers on predicting the future values of certain spatial and temporal fields based on past observations. A real-world application of this problem is found in predicting cargo demand in a temporary storage facility (TSF). Specifically, we are tasked with forecasting the quantity of cargo arriving at TSF per hour based on past cargo arrivals at specific hours. Due to cargo arrivals frequently being close to zero, the problem is considered as a special case of sparse sequential patterns. A practical ST-PL method is developed, which performs effectively in forecasting TSF's cargo demand. Additionally, we propose cargo demand datasets based on the open Maritime Executive Transport file format used by the Port of Rotterdam, which contains maritime transportation data in Amsterdam and Rotterdam. These datasets simulate various scenarios of cargo demand following different distributions such as Poisson, normal, logistic, or a combination of these distributions. A real-world cargo demand following a logistic distribution is also considered as an alternative option. These datasets are available online for public use.

This research focuses on bridging the gap between programming languages employing garbage collection for memory management and those leveraging advanced type systems to ensure memory safety in imperative languages. Historically, garbage collection has been used in functional languages, while type systems have been applied to safeguard memory usage in imperative languages. In the context of languages designed for web development, particularly Raku, this work investigates the challenge of reconciling imperative and functional programming paradigms. The study examines the performance, memory usage, and practical outcomes of the distinct memory management methods, comparing them to C, Raku 6, and Java. The analysis concludes by introducing a Raku extension, called raiburn, designed to provide safe memory management with types, thus contributing to the understanding of how to implement such mechanism in Raku. The raiburn library achieves this by incorporating advanced type system concepts, including type inference, raiburn objects, and raiburn types, as well as raiburn::sys::ref, raiburn::sys::weak, and raiburn::sys::final classes.

The concept of heavy neutral leptons, which account for missing neutrino flavors, has a long and well-established history in particle physics. These particles, predicted by the Standard Model, specifically address the question of what happens to neutrinos after they interact with matter. Researchers consider heavy neutral leptons as the primary solution to this problem, with mass below the GUT scale allowing them to account for all three neutrino mass generations. A specific scenario involving a specific type of interaction leads to the consideration of a new physical quantity, which is then measured in terms of two existing electric charge-related properties under a different theoretical framework. Experiment designers propose two possible experiments that could detect heavy neutral leptons with masses below 0.01 GeV and explain why these experiments are significant, namely the development of a new high-energy particle collider with energies of up to 50 GeV, and the use of a novel large-scale in-lab experiment utilizing the existing existing stockpiles of alkaline atoms such as $^{21}$Na.

Permutation decoding has become more prominent lately, allowing it to take advantage of codes' symmetries in parallel. Furthermore, research has found that by treating permuted polar codes as polar subcodes, the number of applicable permutations in permutation decoding can be enlarged. We have taken this concept a step further to pre-transformed polar codes, including those augmented with cyclic redundancy check (CRC) codes and interference cancellation (IC) codes. We utilize a subcode representation that makes use of the available transformations before the IC process to describe these codes as polar subcodes. As a result, the diversity of applicable permutations in the IC process has been significantly increased. We employ this enhanced permutation decoding in polar codes to attain superior error-correction performance when combined with the CRC code. Moreover, the non-binary polar code designs generated based on our findings also demonstrate superior performance over standard polar codes under the same conditions.

We analyze the post-disruption orbit of OSIRIS-GeOrbit (OGOrbit), a technological demonstration mission designed to operate highly agile and variable yaw capabilities. The spacecraft will closely monitor an artificial target on an highly elliptical orbit with a 253-day period. To maintain a stable field of view (FoV) of $2.8$ degrees, OGOrbit will monitor the target with a changing eclipse duration from approximately 30 to 1100 seconds. The artificial target will be placed in a coefficient with an predicted eclipse period of 30 to 140 seconds. The eclipse period will be determined by the telescope's eclipse period, $t_{\rm eclipse}$, as the telescope's position will always be on the same side of the target. Therefore, we develop a mathematical framework to determine the eclipse period, $t_{\rm eclipse}$, and the Stokes parameters (I, V, L/R) based on the telescope's position. The mathematical framework is first established in an planar environment and later extended to a 3D environment with a perturbation theory. The first application of the mathematical framework is to determine the eclipse period, $t_{\rm eclipse}$, and the Stokes parameters (I, V, L/R) for OGOrbit, and to investigate the influence of specific terms on the Stokes parameters (I, V, L/R) and eclipse period. The mathematical framework is then used to establish a co-adding technique for solving polynomial

This paper outlines the development of a comprehensive theoretical framework for understanding the fracture toughness of solid crystals at their most basic level. Founded on the thermodynamic dislocation theory, it begins by postulating that the behavior of dislocations in these solids must comply with the fundamental principles of thermodynamics. A critical premise is that the fracture of a solid initiates when the apex of a pre-existing notch reaches a critical instability point, beyond which it begins to sharpen uncontrollably. The resulting predictions derived from this model are accurate and consistent with a broad range of experimental findings across different materials, including metals, rocks, and even human bones.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops and extends prior work of Miller and Sheffield by establishing a dual relationship between the concept of an imaginary surface and the Dyson model, initially proposed by Maiorano and Sidoravicius. The model creates an infinite random tangle of interacting random variables. We prove that, under certain conditions, the Dyson model corresponds to a specific imaginary surface pairing when initialized with sufficiently high and similar starting points.

In this research, we address the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in multi-dimensional space with smooth periodic inputs, focusing on constructing global solutions from suitable function spaces. The key achievement lies in expanding the range of applicable function spaces, while maintaining consistency with analytical norms, through an iterative approach that utilizes energy estimates, potentially enhanced by the use of the Littlewood-Paley projectors and other mathematical tools. The method can be adapted to handle more complex scenarios, such as data in larger classes or possibly non-periodic initial conditions.

The verification problem for quantum computation is crucial and challenging, where a quantum server attempts to convince a less computationally powerful classical client that a quantum circuit has produced a specific output. The fastest known protocol for verifying classical results in quantum computation has a time complexity of O(poly(κ)|C|^3), but recent advancements have led to a new, more efficient protocol. By developing new techniques, the complexity has been improved to O(poly(κ)|C|), which is a significant breakthrough. Additionally, the developed protocol utilizes secure quantum random oracles and the existence of noisy quantum encryption. Furthermore, the approach is adaptable to obtain polynomial-time speedup over classical verification, without requiring an exact, precise output from the quantum circuit. The method of noisy quantum encryption used in this research is essential, as it facilitates the secure, private exchange of quantum states, and has numerous applications in cryptography and the field of post-quantum cryptography.

A blockchain system enables secure interaction among parties with conflicting reliability, making it a prime candidate for establishing trust within the Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystem, where its applications extend beyond digital currencies. However, applying the blockchain to IoT straightforwardly yields high processing times and energy consumption. To address these limitations in supply chain management, where various IoT devices operate in parallel, a new blockchain architecture has been developed, specifically designed to incorporate a lightweight consensus protocol, known as LC4IoT. Simulations were conducted to test the performance of LC4IoT and the results validate its efficiency in reducing processing times and energy consumption while remaining resilient to malicious nodes.

Generating synthetic cell shapes realistically can contribute to creating useful cell-like data for training AI systems. However, creating accurate, detailed cell shape models is an intricate process, partly due to the usual voxel-based representation getting overwhelmed by the complexity of cell structures. A better approach involves using signed distance functions, but these also have limitations, such as difficulty in handling anisotropic growth and the computationally expensive creation of detailed, anatomically correct models. To overcome these problems, a new method for synthetic cell shape synthesis is presented, combining a voxel-based representation with a refined SDF model of the cell's interior and surface using a neural network, which is trained on thousands of real cells. By using a latent vector to directly control the cell's morphology through an SDF-based genetic algorithm, precise and detailed shape control becomes possible. Evaluations of the synthetic models demonstrate superior performance in identifying similar cells, both in terms of anatomy and overall look, while a low production cost makes a large generation of models feasible. These advancements lead to the current approach outperforming other state-of-the-art methods in the field.

Blind, low-vision, and other print-disabled individuals still struggle with printed documents. Our goal is to make similar digital materials accessible through machine-readable descriptions, a task we call "accessible by machine." In this research, we want to understand the problem from a new perspective, so we've gathered feedback from individuals who are blind or have visual impairments to shape our project's objectives and ultimately develop a solution.

While BERT excels at modeling bidirectional contexts through denoising autoencoding, its reliance on input masking overlooks positional dependencies, leading to inconsistent pretraining-finetune performance. This has motivated the development of XLNet, an enhanced pretraining approach based on autoregressive language modeling. This method enables bidirectional contextual learning by leveraging permutations of factorization order and, due to its autoregressive formulation, rectifies the limitations seen in BERT. Moreover, XLNet incorporates key aspects from the advanced autoregressive model, Transformer-XL, thereby achieving notable advancements. According to comprehensive testing under similar settings, XLNet consistently outperforms BERT across 20 tasks, including several benchmark assessments, by substantial margins.

We've developed computational models aimed at identifying water absorption in the atmospheres of exoplanets using transit spectroscopy, and when we apply these models to data from the James Webb Space Telescope, we find that a stellar model is necessary to accurately analyze this data. By using the OCÉAN simulation of a typical active star, and varying atmospheric conditions on the exoplanet, we've established criteria for detecting planetary water features, and found that a 10-cm/3 atmosphere stellar model is sufficient for this purpose. However, a 100-cm/3 atmosphere stellar model would cause artifacts to be misinterpreted as water features on the exoplanet, and realistic stellar models should be incorporated into transit spectroscopy to avoid such distortions and accurately interpret the data. Stellar models should also be used to account for variability in the white light topography of exoplanet transits, and to distinguish genuine water features on exoplanets from those stimulated by stellar activity.

We will explicitly construct conformal metrics with constant curvature on Riemann surfaces featuring singularities using ODE derived from a type of meromorphic 1-forms. This approach will have an application in classifying a type of metric with constant curvature on the 2-sphere, specifically those with two conical singularities, which is analogous to a theorem initially established by Troyanov.

Research into the swimming motion of the centipede forficatus near the surface of water-water interface shows it doesn't use its 14 leg pairs primarily for movement; instead of most aquatic animals that move by creating waves along the body, this species moves using waves in the opposite direction, from tail to head. Its low mass and the presence of fluids against its body cause movement dynamics where drag forces overcome inertia, which can be explained using theories initially based on microorganisms. These theories are applicable to larger animals, which has implications for understanding how the centipede's body movements and limb movements contribute to its ability to swim.

The ultimate aim of this project is the creation of highly detailed simulation tools that can accurately model tsunami behavior that is affected by dispersal over long periods. Dispersive models are crucial in situations such as a massive ocean impact from an extraterrestrial object, which would result in high-frequency tsunami waves with a significant spread in terms of energy distribution and frequency. 

Although complex simulations involving the inversions of elliptical equations can produce precise results, they are severely hampered by computational speed limitations using traditional methods. However, researchers have discovered that the fast multipole method can greatly improve the performance of these simulations by allowing the efficient calculation of elliptical equation inversions at an O(N) time complexity, making it feasible to utilize more sophisticated modeling techniques on a larger scale. 

This paper outlines the implementation details of a high-performance MPNN-based solution that leverages the use of a hybrid approach. This approach first utilizes the standard FFT method to approximate a dispersive solution, and then further refines this solution using a more complex elliptical equation inversion model. By employing this hybrid technique, it becomes possible to achieve precise results while minimizing the need for computationally intensive multipole calculations. Additionally, the paper also explores various strategies for adapting the fast multipole method to better accommodate the inherent parallelism of such systems, including the division of code snippets into task-parallel blocks, where each block represents an elliptical equation inversion, and the scheduling of these blocks according to a dynamic runtime model. Recent observations from ALMA and Spitzer have uncovered a population of large, distant galaxies that are too faint to be seen in UV imaging taken by the Hubble Space Telescope. These galaxies have been termed "HST-dark" and a smaller subset has been studied for their properties by analyzing optical and near-infrared data from a specific period and region of space. This research has yielded key insights into the physical characteristics of these galaxies, suggesting they have low star formation rates and are highly dust-enshrouded, with the majority of their star formation occurring outside of their central regions. Notably, their stars and dust are highly concentrated within 5000 parsecs and have a ratio of dust mass to stellar mass of about 0.1%. Furthermore, their stars and gases have been found to be somewhat older, at around 1 billion years, and have relatively low metallicities. What's more, their quiescent and star-forming populations show similar sizes and have similar mass ratios, but the quiescent systems are on average more massive, with the mass imbalance appearing to be driven by more efficient star formation in the blue population. The findings suggest these galaxies have evolved from similar, but more massive, galaxy precursors with the star formation have been controlled by supernovae-like feedback to result in a mass and size balance between the blue and quiescent populations.

By incorporating two topological terms into the Einstein-Hilbert action, we form a novel seven-dimensional theory of gravity. Depending on specific constant values, these terms may be equivalent to a 3-form field equation correction in eleven-dimensional supergravity. The complete equations of motion are subsequently determined. Interestingly, the addition of these terms leaves static, spherically-symmetric black holes unchanged. The new theory also yields AdS_7 spaces, squashed seven-dimensional spheres, and Q^{111} spaces in a Euclidean signature.

In a long and narrow container with horizontal axis, two types of disks with varying and identical sizes are placed on a flat surface. Each disk has an assigned polygence, gauging its size to size ratio, under escapement rules that mimic planetary motion. This experimental model mimics the Kepler equation, resembling the two-body problem with gravitational interaction, but only for particles with specific mass ratios, allowing five-fold polymorphism for one type of disk and monogamy for the other. As a given area is occupied, optimization in configuration yields maximized polygence for its configuration stability, with its characteristics analyzed through numerical simulations such as polymerization, jamming, and the study of macrostates with various disk size distributions under constraints, including a normalization criterion for its configuration stability.

Research into El Ni\~no's two main flavors - East Pacific and Central Pacific types - has become a significant focus in climate variability studies. Recent investigations heavily rely on statistical techniques such as multivariate analysis, often using a linear model which assumes that all variables have linear connections to the phenomenon's causes. We employ Principal Component Analysis to examine the differentiation between these two types of El Ni\~no in the context of Southern Oscillation Index and Tropical Pacific SST anomalies. We observe that in the 1900-2018 time frame, East Pacific type Central Pacific El Ni\~no have distinct, yet sometimes overlapping characteristics, especially when it comes to analyzing monthly or quarterly data. We also find that East Pacific type Central Pacific El Ni\~no have distinctly various impacts on the globe's precipitation patterns, causing contrasting effects on the amounts of rainfall during different seasons. Our research highlights that relying solely on statistical linear methods may lead to confusing the distinguishing features between these two types of El Ni\~no, resulting in a incomplete or even incorrect understanding of their impacts and patterns.

When materials that don't have a regular structure are subjected to mechanical pressure, the distortion they undergo may deviate from expected behavior, even within their elastic range. The extent of nonaffine behavior, a concept observed in various numerical models, poses a significant challenge to experimental studies due to its low amplitude and localized nature. A new technique is proposed to analyze this nonaffine contribution, involving compensating for waves scattered by a stretched, amorphous material using precision adjustments to the optical probe's wavelength. The successful application of this approach in glass frits verifies that reversible material deformation is possible and thus confirms nonaffine effects within the elastic range. A model has also been developed to quantify how the material's thermal expansion interacts with changes in wavelength, providing estimates for the size and spread of nonaffine movements.

This research investigates a population model, factoring in the effects of stress and environmental pollution, through the lens of optimal control theory, aiming to minimize pollution levels by finding an optimal adult population equilibrium. By developing an explicit solution for the first-order variational equation and associated adjoint equation, we demonstrate that the optimal control can be identified without relying on exponential stability, which is inherent in the system. Consequently, we derive a explicit transition map to transition between steady-state trajectories, contributing to the broader field of optimal control theory in population dynamics and population dynamics modeling.

The researchers achieve decidability for an infinitely large group of axiomatic extensions to the Full Lambek logic, specifically those with certain weakening and contraction properties. This achievement builds on a previous result regarding the contraction counterparts of these extensions, while the computational complexity was not determined for them. In this study, we introduce just the necessary concepts related to well-quasi-orderings and fast-growing complexity classes, enabling us to provide upper bounds on complexity for the extensions in question. This outcome particularly provides a solution to an open problem in the fuzzy logic community by offering a specific complexity bound for MTL.

Hierarchical taxonomies have immense value in knowledge graphs but their static nature hinders their ability to keep pace with the rapid growth of knowledge graph data. To address this, deep learning-based approaches are being explored to predict relationships based on previously undated classifications. Compared to Euclidean-based models, those employing hyperbolic space are more suitable for taxonomy management due to their natural fit for hierarchical data. Nonetheless, existing hyperbolic-based models are largely tailored towards graph-based data, which is not applicable to single-entity classification tasks. To bridge this gap, a new model called HTE has been developed to leverage hyperbolic geometry for taxonomy enhancement. The results show that HTE achieves up to a 25.5% improvement in classification accuracy over baseline models in multi-label and single-label knowledge graph classification, solidifying its place as a top choice for taxonomy management and hierarchical knowledge graph classification.

A comprehensive analysis of dipolar interaction between pairs of molecules has been completed for all mathematically feasible alignments and intermolecular distances. Our research is based on a third-body approximation, which splits the interaction into three components: the dipole moment along the intermolecular axis, a moment perpendicular to this axis as part of a quadrupole interaction, and a moment that arises as part of a octupole interaction. Since dipole moments are influenced by the significant effects of orientation, by using the free molecular model, we demonstrate that these moments are substantially greater than those associated with the free rotating model. Furthermore, by examining the quadrupole and octupole interactions, which are only noticeable at close intermolecular distances, our results indicate that these effects are practically non-existent except when molecules are very close to each other, such as in solid-state matter. Our findings are derived using analytical equations for various alignment configurations and distance ranges.

The fourth Industrial Revolution has significantly improved industrial productivity, but it is hindered by difficulties in accurately predicting schedule adjustments and budget revisions. Delays in shipments and inaccurate budget assessments in industry are primarily caused by the unpredictability associated with machine learning. A novel non-robust probabilistic interval allocation model based on the most direct paths in a network is designed to provide a single overall estimation of expected costs for multiple parallel processes. This intuitive and straightforward approach simplifies the complex task of simultaneously managing multiple parallel operations with unknown timelines. To further analyze budget unpredictability, we developed a model to generate multiple random budget values based on historical data and calculated variance. By integrating these concepts into a discrete event simulation, we created a comprehensive system to predict overall system performance even in complex scenarios with non-deterministic processing and unpredictable resource allocation. We tested our approach using real-world data from the Renewable Energy Laboratory at the University of California, which helped us quantify the impact of allocation unpredictability on overall system performance.

Cyber-Physical Systems require robust resilience properties to withstand disruptions, yet a standardized approach remains lacking. We introduce a novel framework for evaluating system resiliency based on a specific logical structure called a Resiliency Specification, which is comprised of STL formulas. By integrating time bounds and combining individual components, this framework provides an in-depth analysis of a system's ability to rapidly recover and maintain stability. We provide a measurable Resilience Satisfaction Value, which evaluates resiliency on a scale, considering two key factors: swift recovery from disturbances and sustained stability. The practicality of our approach is demonstrated through the use of case studies, marking a breakthrough in understanding multi-dimensional resiliency, while offering valuable insights for evaluating complex systems.

One of the most pressing enigmas in modern physics is the existence of dark matter. Although it's confirmed that dark matter gravitationally affects luminous matter, this interaction makes accelerometer-based searches particularly intriguing. This article details ongoing and future searches for dark matter particles such as feebly interacting matter trapped on Earth, scalar domain walls, and axion quark nuggets, employing accelerometers in a network configuration and discusses how atomic interferometry-based networks might enhance these searches.

Consider a complete, non-compact Riemannian manifold M with dimension m, equipped with the metric g, whose Bakry-\'{E}mery Ricci curvature is bounded below by zero. We derive a localized version of Hamilton's gradient estimate for the solutions to a nonlinear diffusion equation, which have a positive, smooth, and bounded u. The equation u_t is given by \[ \Delta u - \nabla \phi \cdot \nabla u = (au + b) \log u. \] In our analysis, \phi is a twice continuously differentiable function and a and b are non-zero constants. Our findings extend existing work from Souplet and Zhang (2006) and Wu (2008).

Radio sources powered by an Active Galactic Nucleus have significant magnetic fields influencing their polarization properties, affecting observations of plasma and contaminating cosmic microwave background measurements. Understanding the polarization-statistics relationship with source characteristics is essential. By analyzing large radio source samples from 1.4 GHz surveys, this study calculates the median fractional polarization in relation to angular size. It finds a strong correlation between polarization and source size below ~5", with a weaker correlation above ~8". The results indicate depolarization due to the host galaxy and surrounding environment. Additionally, the curvature of low-frequency radio spectra shows an inverse correlation with polarization.

Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are a type of mathematical model based on Markov processes, but with the critical difference of having an inaccessible internal state, which cannot be directly observed. This internal state can be predicted by observing a probability-distributed output that is influenced by the hidden state. HMMs, which also include initial and final probabilities of transitioning through these states, have found extensive applications across natural language processing, speech recognition, and other fields. The task of one best path decoding is the simplest method for predicting the hidden state sequence in HMMs, which when combined with the most likely observation sequence, results in the maximum probability of the model's path. However, this path decoding method has the drawback of only using the initial observation at each step to determine the model's state, which can be inadequate for dealing with scenarios where the systems being modeled change gradually over time. The use of all possible observation sequences can provide more accurate results, but is only feasible when the number of possible observations is relatively small. The development of techniques such as the best N best path decoding, which keeps the N most likely model paths and their associated observation sequences, has helped to alleviate this issue to some extent. Nevertheless, even with this extension, the decoding process remains limited in its ability to utilise the time-varying information in observation sequences. The use of time-varying HMMs, which incorporate the time-varying information in observation sequences, can provide more accurate results, but

We develop a class of stochastic advection problems to investigate turbulent transport properties, where the flow field statistics are represented as a continuous time Markov process. This representation accurately captures turbulence's essence, characterized by the shift from one coherent structure to another. Our analysis yields exact expressions for the turbulent transport operator without employing simplifying assumptions. In the limit where spatial and temporal locality prevail, our operator reduces to the conventional estimate of turbulent transport as a diffusivity tensor, with its components being the integrated velocity field auto-correlation.

We maintain that many 'good' fits to elastic scattering data are unwarranted,
relying on unsubstantiated geometric survival probabilities from unknown $S$-wave interactions.
To rectify this, we suggest an alternative method for evaluating folding models that should provide a more grounded approach to describing nuclear elastic scattering.

This paper presents an alternative derivation of Einstein's radiation theory, showcasing the non-sequential thermodynamic behavior of electromagnetic radiation in a thin slab at low temperatures. The usual gas thermodynamic properties are replaced by an electromagnetic radiation-specific set that incorporates a frequency-dependent factor. The unconventional radiation behavior is most pronounced in a transition region of low temperatures, spanning a very narrow interval. The radiation energy density and related variables exhibit a shift of up to three orders of magnitude. The observed phenomenon is attributed to Einstein's initial application of quantum rules to electromagnetic radiation, dating back to 1905. His theory on radiation was followed by the groundbreaking paper on the photoelectric effect, both contributing to the emergence of quantum theory.

Protecting users of location-based services with significant privacy requirements is extremely difficult when multiple locations are shared within a short time frame due to the significant relationships anticipated between these locations. Our proposed R\'enyi divergence based framework measures and bounds expected privacy losses for interrelated data sets, further demonstrated through a new location-based privacy metric. This framework was applied to a widely used min-angle-based location perturbation method to modify it and enhance its privacy properties. Evaluations using simulated data confirmed that our approach successfully eliminates the significant risks of privacy leakage caused by disclosing interconnected location data. This modified technique is then tested using real GPS data and shown to provide significant privacy gains while maintaining similar distances to desired locations for users.

A highly sought-after component in autonomous driving, 3D lidar-based place recognition excels in areas lacking GPS or experiencing interference. However, due to a lack of suitable data over 2D image representation, research has primarily focused on feature quantization for place recognition, albeit underoptimal. Our work addresses this by introducing the LiDAR-based Cyclic Rank Autoencoder (LiCRA), a novel model leveraging 3D cyclic rank operator cyclic-associative memory (CROM) to create an efficient, lidar-specific place recognition system. Our findings demonstrate LiCAR's ability to outperform current methods, as seen in our publicly available dataset and benchmark. The code can be accessed at https://github.com/fateck LiCRA.

Research has shown that combining resting-state functional MRI data from multiple sites can potentially introduce systematic biases in connectivity measures. In this research, we studied how site-to-site effects impact our ability to detect individual and group differences, and our analysis suggests that multisite studies are feasible when utilizing large sample sizes. Our data collection was based on actual, rather than simulated, fMRI datasets from N=345 young, healthy subjects, gathered across eight sites, all of which utilized 3T scanners and consistent scanning protocols. Our sample consisted of males and females, and we utilized sex as our comparative variable. Our findings show that multisite effects have a minimal impact on connectivity, and our detection power for sex differences remains significant, even when incorporating data from multiple sites. Crucially, our results suggest that, as the sample size reaches N=350, including data from multiple sites becomes viable without compromising our ability to detect sex differences.

In a single-hop beeping network, stations interact via one-bit messages to form a distributed communication system. We explore the distributed computing domain's two core challenges, naming and counting issues, and our objective is to refine existing algorithms to reduce their energy usage and processing speed. Our key contribution is the development of efficient, randomized algorithms that achieve optimal O(n log n) processing efficiency and O(log n) energy usage for n-station beeping networks, addressing both the naming and counting problems.

Recent advancements in NLP for code-mixed languages have been hindered by the lack of suitable word representations. We have developed a novel method for creating these representations, starting with a page rank-based model that incorporates two types of transition probabilities. This method combines monolingual and bilingual n-gram models, which are themselves generated through neural machine translation systems and language models. We utilized this method to create word representations for two code-mixed languages and both native languages, and subsequently developed models for sentiment analysis, topic modeling, and language identification. The resulting models' superior performance highlights the efficacy of our approach.

Using a combination of density functional calculations and the linearized Migdal-Eliashberg equations with the functional derivative approach, we studied how the density of states affects the behavior of H3S as a function of pressure between 166 and 250 GPa. Our results show that accounting for the variable density of states significantly improves the match with experimental data for the critical temperature of H3S, reducing discrepancies at higher pressures. Additionally, we found that considering the variable density of states enhances the stability of theoretical predictions against variations in the interaction strength. While our calculations indicate that the interaction is primarily repulsive, we found that short-range and long-range components behave differently, with the former potentially being a mixture of attractive and repulsive forces.

This paper presents an innovative technique to create spatial boundaries for navigation in dynamic environments. In the past, motion planning methods have struggled with fundamental limitations in environments that change over time, such as dynamic traffic or areas with significant disruptions. Typically, global planning methods have assumed static environments, hindering their effectiveness and efficiency. To address these limitations, we developed an innovative approach to constructing spatial boundaries for navigation in dynamic environments, utilizing an experience replay mechanism and an artificial neural network to update and optimize these boundaries efficiently. This method demonstrates superior performance, significantly outperforming existing methods, as showcased through experiments in simulated environments and real-world navigation scenarios.

This research proposes a visual relocalization method based on geometric information derived from 3D surfel mapping. A comprehensive database of images is initially created by grouping similar image features based on their appearance and3D positioning. When a query image is processed, its features are matched with those in the database by considering their spatial relationship. To enhance both accuracy and efficiency, a multi-stage image-to-image comparison approach is employed, where previous database images are progressively eliminated from the search pool. Furthermore, a probabilistic model is used to rank potential matches, and the top-ranked ones are selected for a final precise alignment. Experiments conducted on existing datasets demonstrate that the proposed method is at least equal to, if not better than, existing surfel-based relocalization approaches. To facilitate comparison and evaluation, the proposed method, along with necessary data and code, is made publicly available.

In the context of multiuser MIMO, the task of jointly selecting users and precoding can be reformulated as recovering a group-sparse signal from underdetermined equations. Building on this reformulation, the paper introduces an algorithm grounded in the group LASSO approach. Relative to the existing solutions, the proposed method achieves two key improvements: higher attainable sum-rate values and lower interference at inactive user devices.

We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve has an equivalent representation as a finite-dimensional simple algebra over the tropical semifield extended by a single element.

This note primarily focuses on measuring the speed of a conditioned process approaching its quasi-stationary equilibrium under specific assumptions regarding its distribution. In reverse, we establish that a conditioned process converging uniformly to a self-conservative, ergodic Markov process also attains a distinct quasi-stationary equilibrium, which it converges toward at an exponential rate across all initial distributions. Furthermore, we illustrate a corollary ergodic theorem under specific conditions.

We've demonstrated that combining the 1-cocycle of a long knot's space with Fox-Hatcher 1-cycles produces a Vassiliev invariant, having a specific order of n. This invention surpasses earlier Vassiliev cocycles developed using chi-bar and delta_p. As a result, a long knot's space fails to support the established lambda cocycle. The developed 1-cocycle is expressed through the formal link determinant, containing a power series of long knot invertibility operators. Its generating function matches the Volodin invariant, a renowned Vassiliev invariant of order infinity. Furthermore, correlation with the Volodin invariant suggests a long-standing conjecture that a long knot's space is asymptotically free.

The connection between unconventional superconductivity, antiferromagnetism and nematic order in iron-based superconductors is still the subject of controversy. While in most FeSCs superconductivity arises close to a nematic and magnetic state, the iron-based compound LiFeAs exhibits unique characteristics, becoming superconducting below 18 K without undergoing a magnetic or structural phase transition. Some studies have hinted at the existence of nematic fluctuations and a nematic superconducting state in LiFeAs, but recent findings from this study indicate that pristine LiFeAs, along with LiFeAs doped with low levels of Co and V, show no signs of being close to a nematic instability, which contrasts with the findings in magnetically and nematically ordering NaFeAs.

This research reviews a global analysis of Type-II two Higgs doublet models and considers how upcoming measurements of the SM-like Higgs and Z-pole may influence allowed model parameters. Based on a global analysis of two Higgs doublet models using the GAMBIT tool, our study takes into account a broader range of constraints than previous assessments, including limitations on dark matter direct detection experiments, precision electroweak observations, and cosmic microwave background measurements. We also introduce new features to our analysis, such as restrictions on $m_{h_1}$ and $\tan\beta$ derived from late-time cosmic deceleration and Big Rip phenomena. Furthermore, our analysis evaluates compliance with Lyman-$\alpha$ forest observations and the cosmic microwave background measurements of the relic density of dark matter.

We demonstrate through simulated molecular surface experiments that neuroevolutionary learning can independently design particles and temporal strategies for enhancing spontaneous assembly processes, based solely on the desired end properties and specified structural characteristics, and not relying on pre-existing understanding of the physical laws or possible material configurations. This algorithm can effectively pursue both goal-oriented and open-ended design approaches, enabling it to either produce a material with user-defined features or explore and discover new structures within a specified set of constraints. In this exploration mode, it delves into the range of possible materials and structures that can be formed rather than merely identifying those that are thermodynamically favored or stable over time.

Our research appears to suggest a dynamical-Higgs-phase outcome in a broad range of chiral gauge theories, particularly those that are strongly-coupled. In contrast, a different scenario featuring flavor symmetric vacuums with massless baryonlike composite fermions does not seem as likely. The possibility of formulating a strong-anomaly effective action, similar to one applied to QCD with a certain number of quark flavors, is another key advantage of the proposed dynamical-Higgs-phase solution, thus offering new avenues for theoretical and phenomenological investigations.

This paper seeks to establish the healthiness of the Navier-Stokes equations under  Lq  type conditions in a critical space, specifically where  1 ≤ q < 2. For dimensions d greater than or equal to 3, this investigation explores whether solutions to the stationary Navier-Stokes equations are unique in a critical space, specifically where  q  is between 1 and 2  (not equal to 2). It has been previously established that this is the case when  q  is greater than 2. Conversely, in cases where  q  is less than or equal to 1, this problem remains unresolved. This analysis also examines whether solutions to the stationary Navier-Stokes equations are regularized in a critical space, specifically when  q  is between 1 and 2  (not equal to 2). It has been previously established that this is the case when  q  is greater than 2. Conversely, in cases where  q  is less than or equal to 1, this problem also remains unresolved. We have studied how the polarization of magnon modes in specific antiferromagnetic systems changes when these modes strongly interact with each other. To achieve this, we have employed three techniques: calculating polarization through the inverse of the susceptibility tensor, applying the Stancil-Feenberg method, and analyzing the symmetry of the magnon eigenstates. Our research focused on a particular type of antiferromagnetic arrangement, which can be easily transformed into a different electronic configuration by applying external voltage. This has allowed us to identify how the polarization of magnon modes is affected by various electronic arrangements, and has led us to discover a significant increase in polarization when moving through specific transitions between these configurations. Our findings are particularly significant because they show that magnon polarization can be controlled and manipulated through these electronic changes, and could potentially be used in novel magneto-optical devices that can be controlled electronically.

This research introduces two modifications for enhancing the security of Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem.
Originally built using Gabidulin codes within the McEliece framework, Loidreau's system is now susceptible to a polynomial-time key recovery attack under certain circumstances. To counter this vulnerability, we suggest employing subcodes to conceal the secret codes in variants of the system, utilizing parity-check matrices derived from random symmetric matrices or Bernoulli matrices. By utilizing the covering radius bound, we confirm that our proposed secret codes possess sufficient security, as they are immune to key recovery via information-set-recovery attacks, including the quasi-correcting property. Consequently, we are able to provide a lower bound on the computational complexity required to break the modified system, specifically stating that any algorithm requiring less than sub-exponential time can be identified and eliminated. Furthermore, we provide a performance analysis of our proposed modifications through numerical simulations, showcasing a practical implementation of our system, including a comparison with other code-based cryptosystems.

To improve pre-trained language models (PLMs), which are trained on large
datasets and generate general word meanings, researchers are exploring new ways
to enhance model performance. The quality of these word meanings depends on how
often the words appear in the data, leading to underoptimized representations of
infrequent words. This paper investigates a novel method to address this issue by
leveraging dictionaries like Wiktionary to define rare words. The rare word's
definition is added to the input text, along with two novel tasks: word and
sentence alignment. This enhanced model, Dict-BERT, is evaluated on various NLP
benchmarks and shows significant improvement in processing rare words and
overall performance on NLP tasks.

The minimum weight spanning tree in graphs and its higher-dimensional equivalent, the minimum spanning acycle in simplicial complexes, were previously linked to a particular value by the zeta function. A recent study of these structures focused on the expected weight convergence. In this work, we investigate the distribution of weights of a minimum spanning acycle when only partial data is available. Our findings include that the empirical distribution of acycle weights is connected to the structure that results when complementary parts are analyzed and that extreme weights exhibit Poisson distribution patterns. These results have an application to the study of persistence diagrams used in topology, where they can inform about times of change in data patterns.

In this context, we explore a privacy-preserving approach called federated learning that allows various entities to train a joint model without exposing each other's data. There are two primary types of FL, namely horizontal and vertical FL, which differ fundamentally in the data available to them. While horizontal FL operates with the same data structure across participants, the structure is unknown in vertical FL, which makes it popular for applications such as data mining, the Internet of Things, etc. To apply the FedSGD algorithm in scenarios where the data is not uniformly distributed, we suggest a multi-level Federated Learning approach. To achieve this, we first combine the data with the aid of hash functions in vertical FL and then utilize the Benign Stochastic Block Relaxation algorithm to address the non-uniform data distribution in horizontal FL. Our proposed method is evaluated based on synthetic data representing real-world non-uniform data distribution. The results show that our proposed approach results in models trained using the FedSGD algorithm that surpass those trained locally by individual participants, with a loss in performance of less than 3% on average compared to central training. Furthermore, the computational efficiency of our approach is substantially improved, enabling the internal reuse of computation between FL iterations.

A theoretical framework called B-Mesogenesis, which involves hypothetical dark matter components, forecasts specific decays of B mesons. Researchers propose a new method for determining the amplitude of the primary type of such decay: B+ particles breaking down into a proton and an antiparticle composed of dark matter, known as the Psi particle. By using data from QCD light-cone sum rules, they analyzed how B Mesons transition into a proton, taking into account two distinct models related to B-Mesogenesis, and they quantitatively assess the likelihood of such a decay occurring in relation to various masses and the degree to which it is influenced by the presence of the Psi particle.

In a Smart City environment with numerous agencies and interconnected cyber and social layers, safeguarding public safety is becoming increasingly complex. To address this challenge, this study develops a sophisticated mathematical model that simulates the interactions and resource allocations between agencies when faced with terrorist attacks on both physical and cyber-social targets. The proposed model, Smart City Defense Game, considers the interactions among three players, each having a limited budget, as they defend their territories from a common enemy, the Terrorist Organization. Each layer includes multiple targets, and the defense outcome depends on the relative allocation of resources by the respective agency and the Terrorist Organization. Players can reallocate their budgets for mutual benefit. We have fully identified the optimal strategy, Sub-game Perfect Nash Equilibrium, which outlines the best possible resource allocation among agencies and the Terrorist Organization, given the terrorist's attack on any single agency's layer. The effectiveness of our model is demonstrated by numerical examples that show the optimal resource allocation among agencies and the resulting outcome based on the terrorist's attack on any single layer. Furthermore, the model's potential applications in identifying vulnerable targets in a Smart City environment are explored.

Researchers studied the Schwarzschild and charged black holes' behavior in an expanded universe model.  They considered these black holes within a large empty sphere of radius $r_B$ in an expansive space environment. Contributions to the thermodynamic properties of the black hole from the sphere's volume were also taken into account. Utilizing the methods of statistical mechanics, they demonstrated that the critical temperature $T_c$ of the black hole is directly related to the sphere's pressure $P$ as well as its radius $r_B$. Specifically, they found that the critical temperature $T_c$ is half the value of the sphere's pressure $P$, and they also found that the critical temperature $T_c$ is directly related to the sphere's radius $r_B$. In order to further understand the relationship between the sphere's radius $r_B$ and thermal transition, they graphed the thermodynamic properties of the sphere's radius $r_B$. These findings provide new insights into the relationship between the sphere's radius $r_B$ and thermal transition. Additionally, they compared their results with the theoretical and experimental data of the universe's thermal transition.

Long document retrieval has been a longstanding difficulty in reading comprehension, with recent advancements in language models beginning to address this challenge. Nonetheless, a significant obstacle persists in processing lengthy, semi-synthetic documents found in datasets such as LongSummary, and in cases where entire sections or paragraphs must be weighed in the retrieval process, rather than just specific sentences. We address these limitations with our proposed product ranker, which incorporates a BERT-based reading comprehension model to improve the accuracy of long document retrieval, and also proposes two new, novel datasets: LongDocument and DocRanking. Extensive evaluations of the proposed model have been conducted on five publicly available datasets, including two new ones, and have demonstrated the model's superiority over multiple baseline techniques and a leading reading comprehension model.

Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with an extremely limited number of labels. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling technique is often employed to mitigate this issue, which aims to supplement the training set with high-confidence, pseudo-labeled nodes in a self-training process. Nevertheless, current pseudo-labeling methods struggle with labeling nodes on large-scale graphs in a short period of time. To address these concerns, we have developed an innovative pseudo-labeling framework that labels nodes efficiently on large-scale graphs with a limited number of labels. This framework combines local consistency constraints in graph classification, adaptive threshold adjustment, and a scoring function to refine pseudo-labels, which are then used in a self-training process to enhance the model's performance. The proposed framework outperforms current pseudo-labeling methods in various scenarios, requiring fewer anchor nodes to achieve comparable performance, and significantly speeds up the labeling process on large-scale graphs with a limited number of labels.

Betatron radiation spectroscopy in a focused plasma column can serve as an efficient, non-invasive tool for analyzing the dynamics of plasma wakefield acceleration experiments and electron beam dynamics. This research demonstrates how analyzing the spectrum of betatron radiation emitted by witness electrons in a plasma slab with varying electron densities can provide precise information about the initial conditions of the witness electron bunch and the dynamics of the driving beam. Such insights are crucial for dissecting the dynamics of beam-plasma interactions and uncovering reasons behind driving beam and witness electron bunch on-axis density discrepancies, potentially revealed through betatron radiation spectroscopy.

This study introduces the first fully verified methods for privately learning decision trees in a hierarchical manner across a network of devices. The proposed algorithm, DP-TopDown, provides secure tree learning and presents two decentralized variations. The initial approach, NoisyCounts, applies a privacy mechanism by incorporating random noise. The alternative method, LocalRNM, reduces noise transmission by optimizing local data processing. The analysis demonstrates the first secure guarantees for privately trained decision trees on both individual machines and network configurations, highlighting the importance of a large dataset. The research further showcases the interplay between data security, accuracy, and tree applicability in decentralized environments using real-world datasets.

We focus on the variational inference task of minimizing a R\'enyi divergence regularized with a constraint in the context of exponential families, and introduce an improved moment-matching algorithm, incorporating a proximal optimization step. Leveraging the information-geometric connection between Bregman divergences and Kullback-Leibler divergences, the proposed algorithm is equivalent to a Bregman proximal gradient method, offering the flexibility to apply geometric insights from the approximation while using black-box stochastic updates. Building on this perspective, we provide rigorous theoretical justifications, including proof of monotonicity and convergence to optimal solutions, as well as an in-depth analysis of the algorithm's asymptotic tracking directions. Moreover, the algorithm's efficiency is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments.

This generalises the discrete Bayesian network class to the chain event graph class, retaining the Bayesian network's benefits for interrogation, propagation, and learning, but allowing for more organic modelling of unordered events and their sequential nature. This paper illustrates how product Dirichlet priors facilitate full model sampling with closed-form conjugate analysis, proving they characterise suitable homogeneity assumptions within this expanded model class. It showcases this capability with two educational illustrations.

In studying Tikhonov regularization for convex minimization problems, we've found a way to tightly bound the set of minimizers without the second-order conditions typically required. This discovery allows us to apply the regularization to problems that only have weak second-order conditions, and it also facilitates a more streamlined analysis of problems with Legendre functions in their objectives. Furthermore, our approach has been extended to cover Fenchel-Young constrained optimization problems, and it takes the form of a sharp inequality involving the proximal point map, with potential implications for variational analysis and optimization research.

This study investigates how basic autonomous entities akin to Braitenberg vehicles can manifest complex, unpredictable movements in confined environments. Notably, their behavior around obstacles resembles that of humans with Parkinson's disease, which exhibits severe movement disorders but normal cognitive function. These agents' dynamics resemble that of a damped oscillator, with their near-wall dynamics explained by a mathematical superposition model. This framework also predicts the emergence of three distinct patterns of movement around a wall: circular trajectories, temporary fixation near a wall, and prolonged periods of wall-proximity. Furthermore, our model demonstrates that these characteristics arise not only in environments with simple geometry but also in environments with varied shapes and sizes. Interestingly, even though these systems are deterministic, their dynamics resemble random processes, with the supposition that their activity corresponds to a random telegraph process. Our findings suggest that even simple autonomous systems can manifest a broad array of movements, including those resembling extreme disorder.

Within the framework of the kinetic energy driven superconductivity theory (KEST), an analysis is performed of the response to a microwave field in cuprate superconductors. Considering that electrons in different energy sectors exhibit varying response times to the microwave field, a hierarchical approximation is used to study the interaction between photons and electrons. It is found that the phase lag of the carrier current in relation to the microwave field displays non-Fermi liquid behavior, resulting in an complex expression for the microwave conductivity. By evaluating the contribution from each energy sector, the kinetic energy driven superconductivity is shown to demonstrate $\Delta_{sc} \propto T_o^{2\gamma-2}$ where the exponent $2\gamma-2$ is related to the ratio of the kinetic energy gap to the photon energy. For this specific system, the phase lag introduces an asymmetric broadening of the microwave conductivity, resulting in a unique temperature dependence. It is found that the exponential decrease of the mobility with increasing temperature is responsible for the experimentally observed insensitivity of the critical current to temperature variations.

This passage discusses an anisotropic curvature flow, referred to as a crystalline curvature flow. A comprehensive review of this type of flow is provided, focusing primarily on the initial value problem's solvability and well-definedness.

Our survival relies heavily on plants, and they're remarkably adept at adapting to changing environments through a process of gradual modification. Plants reacting to external stimuli offer a practical application of reinforcement learning. Our proposed \emph{Plant-Growth RL} benchmark provides a diverse range of challenges, mirroring the complex behavior of real plants. This benchmark consists of a family of related tasks, rather than discrete, isolated problems. Our benchmark exhibits a unique combination of characteristics: first, tasks are interconnected and varied in a way that's difficult to pinpoint; second, there's a gradual shift between tasks and plant models; and third, there's a contrast between the simple, yet effective, rules governing plant growth and the challenging patterns plant growth displays. Our experiments show that existing RL algorithms that practice task variation without explicit adaptation are able to solve \emph{Plant-Growth RL} but struggle to meet the performance of a custom-trained model for the environment. To address this, we present \emph{EPG}, a method that's capable of analyzing the structure of related tasks, detecting subtle connections between them, and assigning varying levels of importance to different task elements. EPG is designed to handle a continuous learning process and work with complex, gradual changes in patterns. Using \emph{Plant-Growth RL} and related extensions, we evaluate different approaches and highlight the benefits of exploiting task structure and relationships, particularly when working with multiple, related environments. All code and plant-based learning environments are publicly available at

It has been established that the SLE loop measure arises as a natural consequence of combining two Liouville quantum gravity disks through conformal welding when the variable $\gamma^2$ equals $\kappa$ in the interval (0,4). To reach this conclusion, we built upon prior work involving conformal welding of LQG disks, utilizing the crucial concept of uniformly embedding LQG surfaces. When combined with Gwynne and Miller's findings, this result shows that random quadrangulations featuring self-avoiding polygons tend to conform to Liouville quantum gravity spheres decorated with the SLE$_{8/3}$ loop as we scale upwards. Furthermore, this result contributes substantially to a recent study examining the conformal loop ensemble's integrability and also corresponds to a random equivalent of an action functional identity discovered by Viklund and Wang.

The Image Biomarker Standardisation Initiative is a global partnership that strives for consistency in extracting biomarkers from imaging data to enable efficient quantitative analysis. One significant hurdle in this field is the lack of widely accepted guidelines and standards for translating imaging data into high-throughput biomarkers, contributing to issues with study reproducibility. To address this problem, IBSI is working to develop standard terminology, test datasets, and metrics for validating image analysis and biomarker calculations, along with guidelines for reporting results in high-throughput imaging studies.

We have analyzed the effects of including high-spin nucleon and delta resonances on kaon photoproduction using a covariant framework for dynamical routing. This has led to new information about the roles of resonances like the $N(1675)$ and $\Delta(1895)$ in the production of kaons, which cannot be accounted for using traditional low-spin particle physics models based on the resonance routing method by Sullivan. Our extended model also provides new resonance structures that align with experimental data, specifically from the PHENIX Collaboration at Brookhaven National Laboratory, and demonstrate a significant boost in cross section predictions at meson production masses around 1.5 GeV, aligning with observations of kaon meson production at $p$-$p$ collisions at the Large Hadron Collider.

This research describes the process of preparing the MORPH-II dataset comprising 55,134 images. The methodology section delves into the individual steps of the pre-processing sequence, with section two presenting a comprehensive overview of these stages. Section three then details each step of the pre-processing sequence, accompanied by a vignette illustrating the techniques used, expaining how they sequence to form the pre-processing pipeline. Furthermore, this research also explores issues of dataset imbalance and how this affects the age prediction accuracy.

Building upon our previous research in arXiv:2001.07937, we investigate the potential connection between primordial black holes and dark matter, as well as dark matter particles. We demonstrate that if dark matter originates from primordial black holes, a significant portion of them can survive and become dominant components of the present-day universe. Our findings also suggest the possibility that dark matter particles could be generated through the process of primordial black hole formation, where a substantial fraction of them can be produced concurrently with the formation of these black holes.

University administrators and educational researchers are concerned with understanding enrollment patterns at a large scale but often rely on decisions made without a solid analytical foundation for student course enrollment behavior. A probabilistic framework can provide a clearer picture, drawing from multilabel classification and mixture models. By using historical data from a large university, a latent variable model based on the Gaussian distribution was built to learn course enrollment probabilities, offering a diverse set of analysis capabilities and robustness against incomplete data. The model performed favorably compared to other approaches such as deep learning methods, effectively revealing factors driving course selection and allowing proactive interventions to optimize student enrollment with potential applications in enhancement of degree programs.

Within vehicle platooning research, ensuring proper vehicle-to-vehicle distance is crucial. A controlling signal can be established utilizing either the connection information matrix H or C, which represent spatial relationships between vehicles in a planned formation or across the entire platoon. These matrices correspond to different topological structures - the former is based on a ring configuration (residual graphs) and the latter on a linear chain (graph of vehicle interactions). Each topology offers distinct benefits in terms of communication efficiency and fault tolerance, with research focusing on the stability of vehicle spacing in linear formations (H) and cluster-based formations (C) separately. A recent paper breaks new ground by examining the stability of vehicle spacing in formations where the topology transitions from linear to cluster-based, which can occur during vehicle entry or exit from the platoon. To investigate this stability, two control signals are considered: the global signal b built from matrix C, and the local signal d built from matrix H within a given cluster. It is argued that the global signal offers better performance due to its ability to account for vehicle speeds. Two methods for designing these signals are explored - maximum modulus and minimum modulus, which correspond to designing signals with the largest or smallest elements. Minimun modulus signals require a pre-established scaling factor, which can be challenging to determine. To overcome this issue, a proposed signal based on the global signal b is developed, by substituting the elements of b with the minimum modulus signals within each cluster. This method is evaluated in simulations

One of the widely applied optimization methods in machine learning is Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), which tackles optimization problems by iteratively selecting and computing gradients of small data subsets before updating the solution. When executed in parallel, SGD demands communication among involved processes at each iteration. Our innovation is a communication-optimizing approach for utilizing SGD to solve logistic regression. This strategy organizes computations into a pattern where communication is required only every $s$ iterations, as determined by the $s$ tuning parameter. By deriving theoretical bounds on operations count, data transfer rates, and latency, and accompanied by experimental findings, we demonstrate that the newly designed Communication-Avoiding SGD (CA-SGD) can reach speedups of up to $4.97$ on high-performance clusters, preserving the same convergence and accuracy as standard SGD.

Artificial intelligence has become a dominant force in creating online content, with capabilities nearly indistinguishable from reality. While advancements have been made in creating convincing fake content, it lags behind detecting it. Our study delves into generated headlines using the Transformer model, and we develop a simple method to evaluate the authenticity of a headline by replacing its title with a neutral phrase and rewording it accordingly. Our experiments demonstrate that our content-based approach is effective in identifying fabricated headlines. Our findings also reveal that with the use of AI-powered generators that employ encoding schemes such as GPT2, accuracy can be achieved at a 76.5% rate, with the finest tuning of these encoders yielding an astonishing 93.7% accuracy. Our study showcases the simplicity and efficiency of our method in detecting fake headlines and highlights our underlying technical solutions. Our code and content datasets are now available on GitHub.

In polycrystalline, amorphous, and ion-damaged Kitaev materials, we demonstrate
that a spontaneous chiral spin liquid develops. Using neutron scattering and
electric transport measurements on partially crystalline and ion-irradiated
$\alpha$-$Na_2 Ir O_4$, we identify a unique energy scale $\Delta$ and
quasi-particle weight $z$, which align with theoretical predictions for a chiral
Kitaev spin liquid. Additionally, we observe a temperature-dependent freeze-out
of dynamic correlations and an exponential neutron absorption similar to
self-dimerization. Our results for Kitaev materials coincide with those from
antiferromagnetic materials exhibiting spin-liquid behavior, such as
$\alpha$-$Na_2 Ir O_4$, highlighting the universal characteristics of chiral spin
liquids across different energy and disordered environments.

Future large-scale radio interferometers, like the SKA, will consist of numerous antennas spread across the globe, requiring advanced signal processing systems to achieve optimal computational efficiency. Traditionally, real-time correlation of antenna signals has been handled through substantial software systems, often running on specialized computing systems, and relying on sophisticated data flow architectures to ensure performance and scalability. Recently introduced architectures, like the FFT-correlator, offer a significant computational advantage by merging traditional correlation methods with the divide-and-conquer approach of the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), typically implemented in hardware. We now provide an in-depth analysis of implementing the FFT-correlator architecture within the current data processing system used by the SKA Prototype Science Data Processing System, evaluating the benefits of integrating this new architecture into the data flow chain. Our analysis has led to the development of a data processing concept, called the FFT-correlator Data Flow Solution, designed to efficiently incorporate the FFT-correlator architecture into the existing data flow, minimizing computational and storage overhead, and optimizing system performance in the process. We now make public the full design description of the FFT-correlator architecture, along with a detailed assessment of its suitability for large-scale radio interferometry, and the outline of a data processing concept that has the potential to scale to meet the requirements of future large-scale radio interferometers, and their complex data flow architectures.

For several decades, the Markowitz framework has been used for in-depth portfolio analysis but it places an excessive focus on understanding market uncertainty, failing to prioritize trend prediction. While researchers have applied generative adversarial networks (GANs) to generate financial time series, their ability to capture complex trends and uncertainties in financial markets is limited. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel method based on multi-objective genetic programming (GP) to generate multiple conditional financial time series models in a single run, allowing them to be applied for both trend forecasting and portfolio optimization, effectively resolving the 'curse of dimensionality' issue often encountered with Markowitz's approaches. Our proposed method produces high-quality GP-based conditional models that outperform similar models created using the TensorFlow Generative GAN method in multiple aspects, including accuracy, model simplicity, training time and convergence rate. Additionally, our method's ability to create multiple models helps to analyze their diversity and highlights the potential biases in the GP algorithm if not controlled.

We have derived the polarized massive operator matrix element $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$
analytically to three-loop order in QCD for arbitrary values of $N$,
including both single- and double-mass scenarios in the Larin scheme.
Furthermore, the result serves as a crucial transition function for the variable
flavor number scheme at $O(\alpha_s^3)$ and is also expressed in momentum
space for convenient use.

A groundbreaking method utilizing Bayesian neural networks enhances the accuracy of classifying gamma-ray sources. The study focuses on identifying Fermi-LAT blazar candidates, consisting of BL Lacertae objects and Flat Spectrum Radio Quasars. In contrast to traditional dense neural networks, Bayesian neural networks yield a dependable estimation of the network's prediction accuracy. The study investigates the similarities between conventional and Bayesian neural networks, along with the effect of data augmentation. The results of this investigation indicate a high degree of correlation between the two network types.
