The incorporation of data augmentation significantly boosts classification accuracy, with Bayesian neural networks yielding a convincing $>3\sigma$ distinction between BL Lacs and FSRQs in multiple trials. Building upon this work's techniques and findings, similar approaches could be applied to classification and identification in various astrophysical contexts.

Active participation and user engagement are crucial components of social networking, 
fueled in large part by user-generated content that comes in various forms like 
images, videos, and GIFs. However, this content remains inaccessible to many users 
due to compatibility issues with their devices. The primary goal of our project is to 
develop a browser extension that enables web users to create content using alternative 
media formats such as images, videos, and audio, while allowing sharing of this 
content across different platforms like Facebook, Twitter, and Reddit. In addition, 
our project aims to expand upon existing cross-device photo and video editing tools 
to encompass browser extensions, focusing on the interface and collaboration 
features that enable real-time multi-user editing and sharing of this alternative 
content across various platforms and devices.

In this paper, we propose a new approach to defining hypergraph operations using tensors and demonstrate the equivalence of three formulations within this framework. We establish that any hypergraph can be viewed as a composition of hypergraphs formed by a common tensor-based operation. This operation allows us to identify and create novel hypergraph classes, enabling us to calculate various properties and spectra for hypergraphs constructed in this way. We also obtain results on the spectra of hypergraphs by applying our tensor-based method to the Ladder, Kautschy, and Tutte's Singleton hypergraphs, and demonstrate its effectiveness in expressing hypergraphs with both singleton and non-singular structures.

India achieved a groundbreaking success with the deployment and functioning of its first multi-wavelength space observatory, ASTEC, and is now preparing to launch INSIST, a pioneering optical and near-infrared space telescope, which will offer global visibility and coverage, including remote and challenging access locations, by carrying out large-scale surveys to study celestial objects, and conduct in-depth studies to address pressing scientific questions. INSIST's key features and capabilities include its large aperture telescopes, which will be equipped with superior imaging and spectroscopic tools, allowing it to offer high-resolution images and data with exceptional signal quality, and featuring fast, highly sensitive detectors that enable fast and highly configurable observations. INSistent's, a younger member of the Indian space science community, is just starting its first science chapter, and this article outlines the scope and ambitions of the INSIST mission, and introduces its initial science goals, which is complemented by the in-depth analysis of the initial science select committee's findings, which includes large-scale surveys to study galaxy evolution, and deep observational studies to address pressing scientific questions related to galaxy and star evolution, and the initial science goals committee also includes notable space research areas such as observing and understanding cosmic events, and studying planets, stars, and the universe, and the initial science goals of the INSIST mission also includes conducting high-quality, and highly observational studies to develop new research methods and improve space science knowledge, and exploring the potential benefits of INSIST's, a pioneering space telescope, to expand and

In clinical trials involving subjects who receive different treatments and have multiple measurements over time, mixed model repeated measures (MMRM) is often employed to control for correlations among these measurements. Recent advancements have allowed for the use of categorical time in MMRM, but using this approach for various treatment categories can lead to issues such as over-fit and incompatibility with normal distribution assumptions, which are analyzed using standard Wald and normal tests. We introduce a novel method that uses mixed model repeated measures for continuous time in pharmaceutical trials, allowing for its direct comparison with the categorical approach through simulation and a real-world example. This method can be implemented using publicly available R codes, including ones from the phast package.

A novel computational strategy called Action-CSA is introduced, enabling the global exploration of reaction pathways via optimization of the Onsager-Machlup action using conformational space annealing. Action-CSA is capable of finding multiple, multiple reaction pathways in a single optimization process, utilizing an annealing schedule to sample the system's configuration space and determine the most probable reaction pathways. The method's efficiency is validated through successful applications to protein folding, polymer ring fluxification, and cyclization reactions, where it outperforms existing pathway prediction methods by identifying multiple pathways without preassigned endpoints.

This paper focuses on a parabolic variant of complex Monge-Ampere equations and utilizes a PDE-based method akin to Phong et al to derive and establish L-infinity and Holder estimates. Moreover, the paper builds upon an earlier work by by Sun for a related problem involving subprime type equations, and addresses a problem initially posed by Phong, Sturm, and Zhang.

Building on Church encodings in typed lambda-calculi, we plan to develop a new
framework based on automata theory that relates to the study of the expressive
power of regular languages. The key idea involves mapping unknown functions,
based on specific rules using finite automata, and then uses these encoded
functions within transductions, which are already regulated by monoids. The
focus will be on the computational limitations of various operations by analyzing
their complexity in different systems, the lattice of polyregular functions,
and other related sets. The study will also explore unification approaches with the
pre-existing framework of Church encodings, based on lambda-calculi, and other
related sets, such as the lattice of regular functions.

This concise note establishes a relationship between Ito and Stratonovich integrals when conditional measure flow components are involved in the integrands, with the 'correction' term requiring consideration of Lions-type measure derivatives to determine necessary cross-correlations. It positions this framework in the context of SDEs influenced by conditional measure flows, with the special case being obvious under complete measure flows.

This research aims to investigate various types of normal subgroups using a specific topology derived from hull-kernel-type topological spaces. We have made significant contributions by introducing a new class of normal subgroups known as primitive subgroups, examining topological properties such as separation, compactness, connectedness, and continuity in these spaces. Furthermore, our study paves the way for identifying spectral spaces among these subgroups.

This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, a column ranking-based unsupervised schema linking approach is developed to address the limited paired training data in existing models. Additionally, a value filling approach is introduced, where pre-trained language models are used to provide implicit values for query gaps. Our unified framework, named Seq2SQL*, incorporates the advanced schema linking and value filling methods, outperforming current top models by a significant margin on the BeamDB and YellowBox datasets.

In complex multi-robot systems, accurately navigating while avoiding potential collisions between robots is a significant challenge, largely due to the unpredictable movements of fellow robots. To tackle this, our method develops a data-driven strategy where each robot solves a series of optimized decision-making problems, considering the robustness of potential collisions with other agents under various scenarios. By minimizing a critically sensitive parameter, our approach ensures that each robot's path has a high level of safety against avoiding other potential encounters, even in the presence of uncertain and dynamically changing information about the environment and other agents' movements. To achieve this, we employ a distributionally robust optimization technique, which utilizes a set of sampled social force scenarios that mimic various possible ways other agents might move. We then leverage this optimization framework to develop a distributed algorithm that facilitates timely convergence of safety-aware navigation among multiple robots, even when local observations are limited and only reflects their recent history. Our method further utilizes model predictive control to focus on short-term optimization around a mid-term navigation plan that spans a relatively short, fixed time horizon, which is easily extended at each step using solved optimization problems from previous steps. By demonstrating our method on a publicly available dataset of humanoid robots, our results show that our approach significantly improves safety in complex multi-robot systems by reducing the occurrence of dangerous encounters with other robots.

Recent data for the Andromeda dwarf spheroidal galaxy And XXV challenges a previous report of negligible dark matter content. Our research significantly reduces uncertainties by doubling the number of studied member stars. And XXV now shows a distinct dark matter component with mass constrained by velocity dispersion measurements within the galaxy's half-light radius. Our findings reveal a mass-to-light ratio and a metallicity consistent with prior research, but a notably low dark matter density at the galaxy's core, making And XXV an anomalous Local Group member when compared to similar dwarf spheroidals. Further research will examine possible factors influencing And XXV's density profile.

In massive machine-type communications (mMTC), granting numerous users low-latency connections is made possible by non-orthogonal grant-free access with low signaling overhead. This research proposes a novel two-stage detection method using message passing on loopy belief trees (MBPLBT) to maximize the number of successful connections for a given interference-based success probability requirement. First, MBPLBT provides an initial estimate of user signal strengths, then iteratively refines an interference matrix estimate through multiple iterations. This process is followed by a second pass at signal and interference estimation, ultimately yielding an improved estimate of user signal strengths. Building upon existing research, MBPLBT has been enhanced with several innovations, including the incorporation of prior knowledge, the use of logarithmic message scaling, and a hybrid approach that trades off latency for increased successful access throughput. Performance gains over the 3GPP low-complexity search MBPLBT (LCs-MBPLBT) and the low-latency MBPLBT (LMBPLBT) hybrid method, specifically a 2.64% and 2.91% increase in successful access rate for 128 users and 128 iterations, have been realized with 128 users and 1000 simulations.

A few approaches to model the thermodynamic behavior of moist air rely on approximations that can lead to inconsistencies in accordance with the 1st and 2nd laws of thermodynamics. A new strategy has emerged that aims to avoid these inconsistencies by leveraging thermodynamic potentials derived from Legendre transforms of the thermodynamic state function. This strategy is now being applied to both dry and moist earth atmosphere systems, with a focus on thermodynamic systems of a finite extent. It is essential to understand that thermodynamic potentials are a fundamental concept, allowing for a consistent modeling of thermodynamic systems and necessitating a critical reevaluation of the consistency of current modeling practices with the thermodynamic postulates.

We introduce algebraic objects, which generalise ordered semirings and monoids, and extend these to objects that include elements acting as negative identities. An exterior algebra analogue is proposed, which provides a cryptomorphism for matroids, and shows that standard exterior and idempotent exterior algebras can be derived from it under specific conditions.

Research in the area of spoken dialogue systems has started to move away from a strict "listen-and-respond" approach by incorporating systems that directly manipulate spoken input, but the standard format for interpreting these systems (the top N ASR text transcript) still lacks the full information needed to accurately represent the system's knowledge and capabilities. In an effort to address this limitation, a method was proposed for representing the dialogue system's knowledge in the form of confusion networks, which are more comprehensive than the standard transcript and offer a more detailed, error-tolerant, and more easily decipherable format. Confusion networks, which effectively capture a range of possible interpretations of the spoken input, have the added benefit of allowing for direct editing and more efficient decoding, all while retaining the ability to accurately reflect the system's knowledge and semantic meaning. As a result, incorporating confusion networks has been shown to improve user satisfaction by enabling a more direct, seamless dialogue experience, and specific applications of this approach have been found in areas such as semantic search, edited speech generation, and dialogue-based search.

We have computed Joyce's enumerative invariants for semistable coherent sheaves of specific ranks and degrees on complex projective curves, which are a more extensive version of the classical enumerative invariants for vector bundles and a more refined version for a 1-dimensional version using Gromov-Witten theory. First, by using moduli spaces of perverse sheaves, we found a virtual fundamental class that represents points where enumerative invariants are non-zero. Next, by applying a formula for perverse sheaves on a complex projective curve, we calculated the enumerative invariants in terms of intersection numbers of fundamental classes of line bundles, which are a type of refined enumerative invariants. Lastly, we established a correspondence between enumerative invariants for semistable coherent sheaves and those of stable pairs, which includes a 1-dimensional version of a conjecture proposed by Pandharipande and Thomas. This is based on a specific version of a theorem by Inglott and Inglott Invariant Theory, which focuses on a particular type of invariants in the context of quiver varieties.

A critical factor in secret sharing schemes is the count of minimal qualified subsets, as knowing this value results in the richest possible access structure. Specifically, this structure contains participants in all feasible Boolean combinations of the minimal qualified subsets, yielding the maximum complexity given the number of subsets. Every access structure can be considered a subset of this universal structure when having the same number of minimal qualified subsets, allowing for comparison and implication. For instance, if one structure has two minimal qualified subsets and another has three, the former is universally least complex given the same number of subscribers. The first half of this text presents definitions, categorizations of access structures, and their comparisons based on set system CardMinQ. The second part, focusing on the complexity of access structures, examines methods to determine the minimum complexity given a specific number of minimal qualified subsets, and these methods are applied to concrete examples.

To determine entanglement in polarization qubit pairs, we utilize quantum estimation protocols. By applying quantum estimation protocols on various families of entangled states, we can achieve optimal precision in measuring entanglement with specific accuracy standards. Our experiments reveal that, although certain families produce the same optimal precision for entanglement measurement, their estimated state densities differ significantly, explaining why multiple optimal estimators may exist for the same level of accuracy in certain experimental setups. We also connect our findings to real-world experiments by analyzing the production of N-qubit Grover states, which provides insights into achieving optimal precision in such experiments.

The long-lived solitary waves, found in Earth's magnetotail plasma, have their current flow parallel to the magnetic field and originate from turbulence in the near-Earth plasma sheet. Researchers create an idealized 2D model of these waves by incorporating the electron-inertia term into the magnetohydrodynamics equation, accounting for one type of plasma species and both parallel and perpendicular magnetic field components. Electron-inertia magnetohydrodynamics theory predicts three distinct wave types: fast solitons, slow solitons, and undular solitons that result from the combination of these waves. The model uses an analytical approach to determine how these waves are affected by plasma parameters such as density, pressure, and speed, showing that the uniqueness of these waves in the plasma sheet is due to specific conditions in the near-Earth plasma sheet that enable the existence of these waves.

Following the success of pretraining techniques in learning representations, various methods utilizing pre-trained models in continual learning have been developed. Some of these techniques build upon the concept of finetuning pre-trained models, either by utilizing the pre-trained classifier after being adapted to new tasks through finetuning the entire model or by combining the pre-trained features with task-specific models. Conversely, using a frozen pre-trained model in conjunction with random task switching has also been explored. Although it demonstrates simplicity and effectiveness, its theoretical foundations are lacking. In this paper, a new theoretical framework is established for understanding the behavior of frozen pre-trained networks in continual learning. The findings reveal that frozen networks perform well when new tasks are dissimilar from old tasks. Conversely, when new tasks are similar to old tasks, performance suffers. Utilizing these observations, a novel and effective continual learning algorithm is developed, referred to as DREAMer. It utilizes both the pre-trained features and task-specific models in conjunction with each other. DREAMer achieves state-of-the-art performance on both image and text-based datasets. Additionally, analysis of the model weights suggests that DREAMer helps to eliminate the interference that occurs during task succession. A proposed theoretical framework also helps to explain how DREAMer operates. Furthermore, experiments indicate that incorporating more new tasks tends to decrease performance and achieves this by causing gradient interference. Consequently, developing techniques to mitigate gradient interference may be crucial in advancing the research in the field of continual learning.

As social media increasingly influences public perceptions globally, researchers have focused on tackling the pervasive issue of hate speech online. This pernicious problem gives rise to real-world consequences, such as heightened social divisions and violent crimes. Previous studies have employed automated hate speech detection methods, but they often fall short by overlooking broader social and contextual nuances. Furthermore, few attempts have been made to explore the explainability of such automated assessments, although they are critical for grasping the complexities of hate speech and formulating effective social interventions. Our research aims to address these gaps by introducing a novel framework for hate speech identification that takes into account linguistic, psychological, social, and historical context. This framework involves combining multiple AI-driven classifiers with an emphasis on explainability. It consists of three main components: (i) initial classification of hate speech using lightweight models, (ii) detailed assessment by an explainer model, and (iii) post-processing mechanisms. To illustrate the efficacy of our approach, we utilize 96 explainable models and achieve an accuracy of 0.748 with an F1-score of 0.370 and Gmean of 0.685 on our developed dataset, called HESM, which comprises 5700 instances from Arabic, English, and Romanian languages. Our study demonstrates that an end-to-end exoplanet model can be too complex and inefficient for large-scale hate speech identification tasks. Our research contributes to the understanding of hate speech by integrating multiple explainable models and stresses the significance of human involvement

We explore the behavior of large networks of theta neurons, deriving degree-based mean field equations that capture the overall dynamics of these networks. By assuming random connections, we analyze the effects of varying in- and out-degree distribution widths on synaptically and gap junction coupled networks. Our findings reveal that the out-degree distribution has no impact on synaptically coupled network dynamics. Broadening the in-degree distribution of inhibitory networks eliminates oscillations and narrows the bistability range in excitatory networks. Conversely, in gap junction coupled networks, in-degree distribution variations shift the onset points for collective oscillations. Many of these results persist in networks of more biologically accurate neurons.

Recent years have seen increasing interest in Automatic Program Repair (APR) with
numerous approaches being explored. One area of research focuses on search-based
methods, including genetic programming, which involves generating and testing
potential repairs in an iterative process. A novel approach we outline uses
Generative Adversarial Networks, a type of deep neural network, to generate
potential repairs directly in an adversarial manner. This invention is not a
direct extension of existing GAN-based software testing techniques and can be
utilized independently to guide a search-based repair process. We also
demonstrate that the quality of the repairs generated can be enhanced by
incorporating additional adversarial criteria. This innovation combines the
advantages of search-based and learning-based methods, offering a more efficient
and precise solution for APR.

This study introduces a general framework for the capacity region of a complex interference channel with interconnected user pairs, characterized by a collection of interconnected rectangles, with each rectangle defined by paired rates of mutual information. While this formula is computationally challenging, it provides valuable insights into the nature of interference channels and facilitates more accurate modeling of interference in specific channel scenarios, such as when inputs follow discrete ergodic Markov processes. Furthermore, numerical analysis confirms that taking the interference structure into consideration can yield decoding improvements in cases like Gaussian interference channels incorporating convolutional codes. We present a method for achieving theoretical capacity pairs, with simulations indicating the benefits of interference-aware coding approaches.

We aim to broaden the established flow analysis technique, which typically operates within the $p_x$-$p_y$ plane, by introducing flow coefficients based on the angular distributions within the $p_x$-$p_z$ and $p_y$-$p_z$ planes. Introducing new flow coefficients, denoted $u_n$ and $w_n$, in conjunction with $v_n$, reveals these parameters to be highly responsive to the nuclear equation-of-state and interaction time. Our comprehensive multisource model research utilising mid-peripheral gold-gold collisions at a 50-60 AGeV energy level shows that the combined $u_n+v_n$ and $w_n+v_n$ flow patterns are closely linked to the nuclear equation-of-state, with specific non-zero $u_n$ and $w_n$ values corresponding to the soft equation-of-state while a $u_n=w_n=0$ scenario is characteristic of a stiff one. Our findings also indicate that the $u_n$ and $w_n$ parameters are correlated with the number of transverse degrees of freedom in particle motion. This, combined with the nuclear interaction's influence on source geometry, suggests that the $u_n$, $w_n$, and $v_n$ serve as comprehensive indicators of the nuclear equation-of-state.

The timely detection of COVID-19 remains a significant research priority, offering potential advantages in the initial assessment and management of suspected patients, while also reducing hospitalization pressures on the healthcare system. Although significant progress has been achieved in deep learning-based algorithms for detecting the disease from chest X-rays and CT scans, the ongoing pandemic has underscored the critical importance of developing methods that operate without access to imaging technology. In this study, a machine learning model incorporating neural networks and statistical techniques is proposed to detect COVID-19 symptoms from patients' clinical histories, demographic data, and laboratory results. The proposed method incorporates a multi-layer long short-term memory (LSTM) neural network to capture temporal relationships in patient data, in addition to a multi-layer LSTM and convolutional neural network designed to integrate information from multiple patient sources. Notably, the model also leverages a teacher-student framework, utilizing a residual learning strategy and gradient regularization to enhance student model performance and robustness, while also enabling empirical risk minimization through the student model. The proposed method's efficacy was evaluated using 1,473 patient data sets, with the model demonstrating robust performance on an independent test dataset, consisting of a 20% cross-validation subset. Notably, the study includes demographic data as a significant patient factor, offering potential applications for COVID-19 and other infectious disease detection.

A Graph Neural Network (GNN) is an effective space-correlation layer that learns node representations by exploiting local and global patterns in wireless communication systems, including channel propagation, node association, and resource allocation. However, GNNs are limited in their capabilities due to certain constraints such as small trainable parameters and node feature sets, as well as difficulty in modeling long-range relationships. To address these issues, we introduce a GNN-based space-correlation layer called ExpGNN, which incorporates exponential weighting and normalization to easily extend the neighborhood of any node, allowing it to capture complex patterns in wireless communication systems, including delayed or periodic relationships. Furthermore, we propose two alternative implementations of this layer, one using Exponential Weighted Average (EWA) and another using Exponential Weighted Average with a Variable Window (EWAVW), and develop associated neural networks, including EWAGNN, EWAVW-GNN, ExpGNN, and their unsupervised counterparts. In addition, we extend the EWAGNN model to a variational autoencoder framework, including EWAVW-VAE, ExpVAE, and introduce an innovative training strategy for all of these neural networks. Finally, we validate the performance of these methods in a wireless communication system by comparing their performance to that of conventional Wi-Fi, non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA), and a Wi-Fi-NOMA-noma hybrid, and demonstrate the potential of these models to improve node representations, delay, blockage

The threat of homicide death tolls has raised concerns worldwide and demands attention from researchers and government officials, a trend exemplified by the high numbers in Brazil, where homicides have become the primary cause of death for people in the 15-39 age group and the third overall leading cause of death.  In evaluating ways to forecast such violent crimes as homicides, murders, and assaults, we found that using historical data from police databases and applying advanced statistics and data analysis techniques has yielded the best results so far.  Utilizing the time series analysis methodology of the ARIMA type and incorporating an component to account for trends, we were able to develop models which demonstrated significant statistical validity and considerable accuracy in the prediction of short-term homicide statistics such as counts and rates.  Our study's predictive models have shown potential applications not only for use in the development of predictive tools but also in the guidance of pro-active policing activities.

Our goal is to modify stochastic gradient descent (SGD) to be adaptable to both 
smooth convex and non-convex objectives by incorporating variable step-size 
mechanisms. We examine and compare the performance of three step-size variants: 
exponentially decreasing steps, polynomially decreasing steps, and step-sizes 
informed by online estimates of local smoothness. When applying the first method to 
smooth, strongly-convex functions, we achieve a convergence rate of $O(1)$. For 
a more general scenario that includes non-convex and smooth objectives, we establish 
a convergence rate of $O(1)(\log N)^{1/2}$. For a polynomially decreasing 
step-size, we can even achieve a convergence rate of $O(1)(\log N)^{3/4}$. For 
the third method, we found it performs well on non-convex and smooth objectives with 
a convergence rate of $O(1)(\log N)^{3/4}$. We take a different approach for 
non-convex objectives under H\"older smoothness conditions, which results in a 
convergence rate of $O(1)(\log N)^{1-1/(2\alpha})$. For a specific case of 
$\alpha=2$, this gives us a convergence rate of $O(1)(\log N)^{1/2}$.

Axions emerge as a logical outcome of the Peccei-Quinn mechanism, the leading explanation for the strong-CP issue.  Variants of axions known as axion-like particles (ALPs) also arise in various modifications of the Standard Model, particularly in string theories.  Both axions and ALPs have compelling justifications as potential components of Dark Matter (DM), and substantial efforts are being made to identify and study them through experiments.  As a result, anticipated axion productions in experiments are extensively examined, whereas there has not been a thorough analysis of expected ALP productions until now.  In this research, we assess the current state of anticipated axion and ALP productions in all current and forthcoming experiments, covering photo and collinear axion/ALP productions, and discuss future projects.

The occupation number over time is examined for a bosonic oscillator coupled to heat baths with fermionic and bosonic components. This oscillator, having one or two degrees of freedom, lacks equilibrium and undergoes decoherence. Such a system serves as an example of dynamic memory through the incorporation of unstable states, or "snakes." It also highlights the limitations and capabilities of this dynamic, along with its implications for the minimum error when measuring position and momentum, and the rate at which "snakes" decay.

Developing robots with skilled hands that can effectively grasp and manipulate objects is an essential yet complex challenge. In comparison to other object-grasping fields, dexterous grasping has been understudied, mainly due to a shortage of extensive datasets. To address this issue, our study introduces DexGraspNet - a large-scale simulated dataset - designed specifically for robotic dexterous grasping: using a robotic hand as the sole grasping agent to interact with diverse objects. By utilizing a multi-faceted approach, we employed various techniques to identify suitable grasping candidates, and performed comprehensive object manipulation to annotate the grasping poses. The data is represented as 3D point clouds and includes both grasping candidates and object manipulation sequences. The dataset is complemented with tools, such as a user-friendly interface, to enable access to the data and a comparison method incorporating a pre-trained model. The latter significantly accelerates dexterous grasping research. With access to a powerful graphics processing unit and a unique setup, our study was able to simulate millions of grasping candidates and object manipulation sequences, breaking new ground in dexterous grasping research. The dataset is available at http://dx.graspinglab.org.

A novel approach is presented for creating and processing four-dimensional (PD-MRI) images with no need for breathing halt. This method transforms MRI into a non-invasive tool for monitoring abdominal organ movement. To achieve this, 2D MRI images are linked together in a specific order, creating a detailed 3D picture of abdominal organs shifting with breathing. To address respiratory movement, a novel T2-shim technique is developed with a unique spatiotemporal control, allowing a stable MRI signal despite changing organ positions. This technique creates detailed, motion-free PD-MRI images by correcting organ movement between breaths. To produce an accurate sequence of still images, a unique method is developed for tracing organ movement, using a detailed 3D picture of abdominal organs shifting with breathing. To test the proposed method, a computer simulation is carried out on MRI scans of the liver from 100 people to evaluate its effectiveness and accuracy in creating detailed, motion-free PD-MRI images with no need for breathing halt.

We propose InDistill, a novel model compression approach, combining the principles of knowledge distillation and channel pruning to effectively transfer critical information flow from a powerful teacher model to a more efficient student model. Unlike previous techniques that collapse this information, InDistill leverages layer-wise pruning of the teacher's intermediate stages, aligning their widths with those of the student, thereby allowing direct information transfer without the student undergoing self-training. Inspired by anatomical pruning, InDistill employs a weighted structural loss to replicate the teacher's multi-stage structure, facilitating the information transfer process. Experiments conducted on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate InDistill to be an advanced method for compressing neural networks, particularly when compared to conventional channel pruning and knowledge distillation strategies.

Two submersion functions from the set of two-dimensional real numbers to the set of real numbers are defined, and their respective level set foliations are examined. The equivalence of these functions topologically implies the topological equivalence of their foliations. Conversely, this relationship does not always hold, as it depends on the local differential of the functions in question. The problem is then generalized to the case of surjective mappings with codimension one, and the topological properties of their regular foliations are investigated.

Ecosystems that naturally thrive in dry environments have become increasingly vulnerable due to the rising threats of degradation and declining productivity. One common method used to assess the well-being of these ecosystems is through analysis of remote sensing data. Researchers employed a multi-scale machine learning approach, using data from NASA's Landsat and MODIS satellites, to analyze the effects of grazing on dry land ecosystems. They combined spectral analysis, spatial statistics, and process modeling to create a geographically-based time series analysis, which was then applied to investigate changes in vegetation, soil conditions, and plant cover over time. Using this approach in two case studies - the Indus Plain in Pakistan and the rangelands of Nevada in the USA - researchers were able to detect how vegetation distribution affects grazing patterns and how these ecosystems respond to them. These findings highlight the potential of integrated geospatial analysis, machine learning, and remote sensing data as a effective tool for eco-systems analysis, land health monitoring, and environmental planning.

A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inliers, exacerbated further when these inliers are highly correlated, resulting in an overly optimistic estimate of the leading dimensions of the sequence. Consequently, a more robust estimator was developed, designed to provide a more realistic prediction. Nonetheless, a new challenge arises in determining the optimal level of robustness, as this is closely tied to the ever-expanding sequence of dimension estimates, creating an inherently recursive and computationally demanding problem. Consequently, this study seeks to address this issue by establishing a theoretical upper limit on the optimal robustness threshold, while also presenting a practical solution based on an investigation of the relationship between the Markov chain and random walk representations of the CountSketch sketch. As an additional contribution, this upper bound is also found to be relevant in a broader context, specifically in its role as an ingredient in a novel technique for providing a more realistic estimate of the top dimensions of a sequence of correlated noisy vectors.

A python-based program, ipie, has been developed for auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo simulations, along with its implementation on central and graphical processing units and interfacing with PySCF. Preliminary timing benchmarks compared to existing C++ codes show ipie performs equally well or better on both CPUs and GPUs. AFQMC results for the isomerization of [Cu$_2$O$_2$$]^{2+} were achieved using ipie with selected configuration interaction trials, achieving convergence for small basis sets. Additionally, results for a quadruple-zeta basis set were approached using green functions. Results for a quadruple-zeta basis set were achieved with green functions, demonstrating good agreement with coupled-cluster results for geometric parameters and energies.

High-frequency trading could greatly benefit from first-generation quasi-quantum communication technologies. This text outlines a simplified game-theoretic approach using the two-player game known as Prisoner's Dilemma. It examines how quasi-quantum communication can expedite high-frequency trading by leveraging Pareto-optimality and backward induction. Furthermore, quasi-quantum communication can enable the implementation of a risk-reversing strategy based on reverse induction, potentially increasing profits. This concept is demonstrated through the strategic analysis of Prisoner's Dilemma, after which we investigate potential applications in high-frequency trading and conclude by identifying areas for future research.

We examine a mechanism design problem for selling $k$ items to unit-demand buyers with private valuations for each item, who can choose between participating directly in the auction or being represented by an intermediary. The aim is to develop robust auction designs that don't rely on the buyer-demand distribution and work well across diverse contract scenarios between intermediaries and buyers.

Initially, we focus on the case of $k$ identical items where buyers draw private valuations independently from a uniform distribution. In this scenario, we design an 'or-or' auction that doesn't rely on the buyer-demand distribution and provides optimal revenue when buyers are represented by low-degree polynomial contracts.

We then consider the case of $k$ distinct items. While the optimal buyer-demand distribution is not known, we develop an 'or-or' auction that surpasses the revenue yielded by the second-price auction, for any given buyer-demand distribution. Additionally, we design an 'or-or' auction that doesn't rely on the buyer-demand distribution and provides at least half of the optimal revenue when buyers are represented by high-degree polynomial contracts.

To facilitate abstractive summarization, we've introduced an efficient planning mechanism that enables the generation of grounded summaries. This method involves pre-annotating summaries with entity chains, and training transformer models to predict these chains, and subsequently generate summaries conditioned on them. In our experiments, which included pre-training and fine-tuning with the new planning interface, we found that incorporating entity chains led to better specificity and coherence of generated summaries. Notably, this approach improved summary fidelity without significant declines in fluency, as measured by human evaluation and automated metrics.

This research presents new sufficient conditions for differentiating a function with n real variables in terms of its partial derivatives based on a related function of n-1 variables. These conditions are applied to establish differentiable criteria for a function with real variables of any finite number, as well as polynomial and continuous functions with real variables.

Vocal synchronization in human conversations plays a significant role in the way
people interact with each other, often serving as an indicator of cognitive behavioral
traits and the depth of social connections. Given its significant social implications
and easy quantification in speech signals, researchers have studied vocal synchronization
in various contexts of human interaction. However, previous studies primarily focused
on simple metrics such as lag and lead, or phase locking values, and failed to capture
the more complex aspect of how people adjust their speaking pace to match each other.
This more sophisticated understanding is crucial to filling the gap between what has
been quantified so far and what is theoretically known about speaking pace adjustment.
Newly proposed measures therefore aim to achieve this gap closure. They are based
on comparing individual speech patterns to a group profile rather than an average
of a group, to determine when speakers tend to deviate from, rather than conform
to, the general speaking pace. Experiments conducted to test these measures involved
analyzing a collection of conversations, using machine learning algorithms to determine
whether these new measures could distinguish between speakers who are highly socially
connected and those who are not as socially connected. Results showed that these
new measures outperformed previous metrics used in similar studies and provided a
more complete understanding of speaking pace adjustment in human conversations.

A recent study applied a realizability technique to establish the meaning of a quantum lambda calculus, which results in a multitude of acceptable typing rules, all of equal standing. Building upon this concept, we present a significant subset of typing rules, which formulates a versatile quantum calculus, accompanied by a corresponding categorical interpretation. Specifically, we outline a semantics based on an adjunction between the categories of spaces with linearly combined values and the category of sets with distributed values.

Analytical calculations have been performed for two types of quasiparticle excitation energies per particle in systems of up to seven electrons within both the Laughlin theory and composite fermions theory, accounting for the comprehensive jellium potential consisting of electron-electron, electron-background, and background-background interactions. The findings support that the composite fermions wavefunction outperforms the Laughlin wavefunction in energy for two quasiparticle configurations, albeit the difference in their energies diminishes with growing system size.

In the context of glaciology, particularly when modelling contact-related issues in plastic deformation, Stokes variational inequalities come into play. This research focuses on creating a robust numerical framework for the mentioned inequalities, utilizing a mixed finite element method combined with a particular lubrication technique called the augmented Lagrange multiplier approach, also incorporating robust numerical integration for the inequalities' residual terms. A comprehensive analysis of the constructed scheme's convergence is conducted and demonstrated numerically on a model ice sheet, specifically at the bed of the Lauteret ice cap, in French Alps, under mechanical contact with the hard substrate of the bedrock.

Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a nearly linear connection between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a significant correlation between outflow mass and gas usage times. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, the mass ejected through outflows actually exceeds the amount of gas converted into new stars, indicating a limit on how quickly gas can be turned into stars due to outflows. Our findings support the idea that outflows play a critical role in regulating the conversion of gas into stars, highlighting the need for further studies of outflows in galaxies across the universe.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at the RHIC and LHC. Contrary to expectations, our findings indicate that both elliptic and triangular flow increase with centrality, which diverges from the predictions of hydrodynamics. We discovered that both flow anisotropies are closely tied to their respective initial forms, with linear Regge phenomenology closely approximating the initial state of elliptic flow but underestimating the initial state of triangular flow. Additionally, our simulation of Cu+Cu collisions at 200 GeV aligns with experimental data on both elliptic and triangular flow. Ultimately, our study highlights that initial geometry plays a significant role in determining low transverse momentum anisotropic flow in nuclear collisions, which must be accounted for in theoretical models.

Our previous work introduced a novel approach to robot swarm systems, incorporating a transparent synchronization mechanism via a'swarm thread' to manage multiple robot maneuvers simultaneously. Building on this foundation, this research expands the foundation by developing a new algorithm to enable swarms of floating service robots to collaborate in tasks within crowded underwater environments. Our innovative solution allows individual robots to compute and synchronize with an optimal swimming speed, thus maintaining a desired formation shape that resists disruption from external obstacles. Ultimately, this enables the swarm to successfully complete tasks such as carrying floating objects and providing visual surveillance within the underwater environment above floating structures like offshore wind farms.

Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires considerable effort,
but a breakthrough has been made in using unsupervised, unlabeled videos for
building a network from scratch. It has been demonstrated that the depth
estimation capability of a network trained solely on videos can lead to a
significantly more accurate semantic segmentation model compared to one trained
using traditional methods. Our work showcases that the depth estimation task is
not only a means to an end, but it can also result in a more robust starting
point for segmentation training than conventional methods.

Let's consider the set of all analytic functions defined within the unit disk in the complex plane and also in the larger disk that has a radius of $1/\alpha$ for some $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1$, not equal to $1/2$. For these functions, we can establish a Bohr inequality, which relates to their 4p-norms. This results in a new class of norm, which we can use to define, along with some additional requirements, a class of functions that are close to being analytic. We can investigate several questions regarding the properties of this new class, which we can denote as $K_{\alpha, p}$ for certain values of $\alpha$ and $p$. We can also explore how to characterize the functions within this class and determine their representation. Furthermore, we can establish an identity of mean values for functions within this class. We can also explore the relationship between the Riesz operators and some other operators that act upon functions within this class.

A nonparametric measure of correlation known as Kendall's tau is examined, along with a more sophisticated variant called partial Kendall's tau.  The latter is defined as the ratio of Kendall's tau to the total correlation within discrete subgroups, which are typically defined by a set of categorical variables.  Both the theoretical and practical aspects of partial Kendall's tau are discussed, specifically with regard to its statistical interpretation, an issue that arises due to the nonparametric nature of the correlation metric.  As an example of its application, the method is used to investigate the partial relationships between species and environmental factors in ecological studies.

Future Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) will heavily rely on Edge Intelligence Systems (EIS), enabling efficient management of massive data from transportation systems. However, current EIS components, including Edge-GPs and the public, contribute to traffic congestion by making uninformed navigation decisions based on incomplete and inaccurate global maps. To address this issue, we introduce EGMAP, an edge-based mapping system that enables decentralized and efficient management of urban road networks. EGMAP, integrated into vehicles and comprised of consumer-grade GPS, camera systems, and the public, calculates accurate and local road network maps while considering public privacy, consumer adoption, and operational costs. In contrast to central map providers, EGMAP promotes decentralization and fairness in urban mapping systems. Our evaluation of EGMAP's accuracy and efficiency demonstrates its suitability for managing and mapping urban road networks. The integration of EGMAP's decentralized approach with ITS and ITS2 can promote equitable and effective navigation, ultimately contributing to the fair and efficient management of urban shared resources.

This study focuses on the application of the Euler characteristic for advanced topological data analysis in multi-variable spaces. Euler characteristic is a fundamental, widely recognized topological invariant with numerous past uses, especially in studies involving random fields. Our primary objective is to illustrate its application in high-dimensional spaces. While employing more powerful invariants like homology remains an active area of research, the theoretical and computational feasibility of the Euler characteristic make it an attractive intermediate step for multi-variable topological analysis. We demonstrate its practicality by using artificial datasets and a real-world example involving diabetic retinopathy detection from retinal images.

Our analysis focuses on an adjusted predator-prey model based on Holling-Tanner's equations with a Type II predation response, also taking into account a strong Allee effect affecting prey population growth. We build on previous studies by Saez and Gonzalez-Olivares and Arancibia-Ibarra and Gonzalez-Olivares who studied similar Holling-Tanner models with a mild Allee effect. In this modified model, complex dynamics are exhibited, including separations in the phase space, resulting in separate regions of coexistence and extinction. Moreover, we establish the presence of a specific type of homoclinic curve leading to the formation of a stable orbit and we discuss potential transitions such as birth-death, oscillatory instability and a doubling bifurcation types including Hopf, Bogdanov-Takens.

The Hirsch Conjecture was a theory claiming that a d-dimensional polytope with n faces cannot exceed a diameter of n - d. This assumption was contested by Santos, whose findings led to the conclusion that some linear programming methods cannot perform optimally within n - d iterations. This series of research was initiated by a novel algorithm, the facet pivot method, proposed in the first paper. This second paper verifies the efficacy of the facet pivot method, confirming it can solve linear programming problems in at most n - d iterations, motivated by Smale's mathematical problem 9, first introduced in the late 90s.

We explore in an associative ring R with identity, the scarcity of k-torsion in the NK1GQ(R), which are Bass nil-groups for general and unitary quadratic groups. Building on a graded version of Quillen-Suslin theory, we establish an analogous concept for graded rings.

This paper undertakes a thorough comparison of the comprehensive, exhaustive approach used in COMPASS computing code with an alternate, simplified representation, introduced by J. Ferreti et al. in EPJ C 81 (2021) 1. The COMPASS computing code is renowned for its meticulous clamping of the two-body mass, ensuring only the two-body state contributes to the off-shell and non-resonant calculations. Conversely, the proposed new scheme omits this constraint, instead relying on a linear off-shell correction to remove its effects from the final results. Our study extends beyond the proton target by incorporating the alpha-induced reactions on a fixed-target and a mobile target, comparing the off-shell corrections for these two scenarios. Furthermore, we assess the impact of mathematical approximations in proposed new scheme on its overall accuracy. The analysis is performed at $x_{B}$ and $Q^2$ relevant for pion-photon transitions and involves single pion production with observed final states containing the pion and neutron/nucleon. In this context, the computational methods' differences result in varying degrees of accuracy in proposed new scheme's off-shell correction for distinct target and observables, ranging from target-dependent effects of up to $\sim$20% in $f_{\pi NN}$ partial wave amplitudes to a maximally 0.35% impact on total integrated cross-sections. The susceptibility of facial recognition systems to fraudulent presentations restricts their adoption in high-stakes applications. Effective countermeasures against these deceptive attempts are vital for the safe integration of facial recognition technology. Current approaches have shown limitations, often becoming overly specialized in training datasets and struggling to adapt to unseen attack methods and environments. In this research, transfer learning is applied from the vision transformer model to tackle the challenge of detecting unknown anti-spoofing attacks. Experimental results conducted on widely accessible datasets showcase the superiority of our proposed solution, outperforming state-of-the-art methods significantly in zero-shot scenarios within the HQ-WMCA and SiW-M datasets, while also achieving substantial improvements in domain adaptation tasks within the SiW-M dataset.

Deep reinforcement learning stands out as a promising AI paradigm for instructing machines via environmental interaction and adaptive learning from their errors. Despite initial expectations, however, its successful application in the automotive industry remains elusive. Following in the tradition of using computer vision for autonomous vehicle development, we demonstrate the potential of leveraging a single 2D LiDAR sensor as both a environment sensor and a training tool using a reinforcement learning approach that is entirely independent of 3D perception. Unlike supervised learning approaches, which are challenged by the variability of driving scenarios and lack of labeled data, we show that self-supervised learning and reinforcement learning can be combined for efficient and generalizable 2D and 3D object detection and vehicle tracking in sensor-specific and camera-independent environments. This is achieved using a novel, self-supervised learning method that converts 2D sensor data into 3D state-space representations for a reinforcement learning agent, allowing it to learn and adapt its 3D state-space action space directly from environmental feedback and drive-based control without pre-existing knowledge. This innovative method also introduces a new modular architecture for a 3D LiDAR sensor that separates state-space from action-space processing, enabling a fully adaptive and efficient learning agent with widespread application potential in areas such as vehicle tracking, object detection, autonomous driving, and robotic motion planning. Our experimental results show that this self-supervised method enables a reinforcement learning agent to efficiently and effectively learn and adapt its 3D state-space action space independently, demonstrating improved

Evolutionary algorithms have seen significant advancements in recent years through parallel computing, leading to highly efficient parallel parallel evolutionary algorithms. However, a major obstacle arises when the evaluation of solutions takes substantial time, causing older generations to be assessed while newer ones remain unseen. As a result, the search performance of these algorithms becomes skewed towards better areas due to bias, ultimately hindering their efficiency. To address this problem, our investigation focuses on parallel parallel evolutionary algorithms and aims to mitigate Evaluation Time Bias (ETB) through two proposed methods. Firstly, incorporating Delayed Generation Selection (DGS) will refrain ETB from exacerbating the search process. Furthermore, the incorporation of a diversity preserving mechanism, such as spatial genetic algorithm, will also alleviate the bias. Through comprehensive analysis and evaluation of our proposed approaches, including experiments with multiple test functions, our results demonstrate that our strategies not only rectify Evaluation Time Bias, but also boost the efficiency and reliability of parallel evolutionary algorithms.

The recent microlensing event OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 involved a cold super-Earth planet located among a group of eleven planet hosts that have had their mass ratios measured through microlensing. We employed to analyze the mass and distance constraints associated with this event, utilizing the observed microlensing light curve and combining it with the constraints from the other ten planets. The mass and distance parameters are constrained by microlensing, indicating a high probability of the star hosting a planet with a mass comparable to Neptune's. By integrating this with the observed mass-ratio power law, we found that $\sim$60\% of the time, a randomly selected planet will be located in a region where its mass grows faster than the luminosity, and slower in other areas. This relationship could help in the analysis of the mass of the OGLE-2017-BLG-1434E planet. The observed mass-ratio power law, however, shows a divergence from the predictions of the standard model, and we found that there is only a 4\% chance that the power law will remain consistent even if the mass of the OGLE-2017-BLG-1434E planet is doubled. The mass of the OGLE-2017-BLG-1434E planet will grow faster than the luminosity when its mass is less than 1.52 $M_\earth$ and slower when its mass is less than $1/M_\earth$.

The concept of an effective, time-independent Floquet Hamiltonian underpins the Floquet engineering of isolated systems, describing their evolution over driving periods and often obtained through analytical high-frequency expansions. However, extending these ideas to open quantum systems, modelled by a Markovian master equation of the Lindblad type, poses a significant challenge. In systems with only two energy levels, distinct phases arise where the Floquet generator may be either Markovian or not. Even within the high-frequency regime, numerical analysis reveals the existence of a phase with a Floquet Lindbladian generator, giving rise to a universal form of the effective Floquet generator. This discovery stems from a general expansion of the two-level Floquet generator, enabling us to write the effective Floquet Lindbladian generator and optimise it for maximum dissipation-free evolution. Our study also explores the conditions for non-universality and the influence of driving and high frequency conditions on the phases of the Floquet Lindbladian generator. Additionally, it examines and optimises the optimal control methods for precise state preparation in two-level systems.

Our recent studies of the effects of Rh content in CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ reveal the emergence of magnetic irreversibilities and spin freezing in the vicinity of x ≈ 0.6, accompanied by a suppression of long-range ferromagnetism. Through detailed analysis of the temperature and field histories, we observed unique characteristics such as non-equilibrium behavior, slow magnetocaloric effects, and significant deviations from adiabaticity. These findings suggest that CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ undergoes a first-order magnetic phase transition at low temperatures.

Using the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Telescope, 19-beam tracking has successfully observed high sensitivity and velocity resolution spectral lines from hydrogen (HI) towards the massive star-forming regions W51 North and W51 East, specifically their HI narrow-line self-absorption (HINSA) layers, which were initially undetected across 21 spillover-coverage. These two regions were then scanned with 241 beams at tandem frequencies to identify and map HI emission and absorption. These regions were further analyzed with polarization full-stokes measurements, with polarization vectors measured for the emission and absorption components. Comparing our 21-spillover data against previous findings from single-dish telescopes, our findings indicate that the massive star-forming regions W51 North and W51 East possessed HI narrow-line self-absorption layers, which were initially undetected across 21-spillover data. These regions were further analyzed with polarization full-stokes measurements, with polarization vectors measured for the emission and absorption components.
