Our analysis investigates the emergence, duration, and outcome of financial bubbles in an environment where multiple types of arbitrageurs interact.  Heterogeneous arbitrageurs interact within the market, inducing stochastic transitions between states.  Initial bubbles are driven by mild optimism, but can also be and foster more extreme speculation.  Notably, optimism typically needs to wane for bubbles to burst, yet increased speculation can sometimes prevent bubble collapse.  Ultimately, market fundamentals serve as the bubble's underpinning, but these may remain hidden from viewers, offering an explanation for the survival of imaginary bubbles in markets and financial bubbles driven by sentiment.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to evaluate the imaginary time Schrodinger path integral for these simulations.

Recent research has shown significant progress in improving recommender system performance through leveraging reviews for predicting ratings, however the current methods have several limitations. The existing techniques often utilize complex neural networks, which make it challenging to easily understand reviewer sentiments. This paper presents a new approach that uses a lightweight model, called LAC-RSVDS, to analyze sentiments in reviews by creating a two-layer parallel RNN model with sentiment and aspect extraction. The proposed method uses a parallel RNN model to separate reviews into parts, calculates aspect-term weights, and then uses user-item vectors to predict ratings. The model also incorporates a sentiment component to rating prediction in order to accurately rate incomplete reviews. Due to its ability to predict sentiments, this method can be used for various tasks such as sentiment analysis, review summarization and aspect extraction. Experimental results on several datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed LAC-RSVDS model on improving recommendations compared to existing methods.

Developing CS NLP systems is obstructed by the scarcity of CS data. This study delves into enhancing CS data utilization using monolingual data, focusing on name entities in CS texts, specifically targeting the name of politicians in L2 and L1 texts, where L2 is the dominant language and L1 is the minority language. The study's primary objective is to identify name entities in L2 texts, given only monolingual L1 documents, yielding CS name entities from L2 to L1 and vice versa. The framework's name detection component is customized for CS, followed by fine-tuning CS named entity detection models to incorporate naming habits from L1 documents. Evaluations were conducted on the Polish-English language pair, producing an F1 score of 29.41 for L2-to-L1 naming and 46.53 for L1-to-L2 naming.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure.

We're investigating integrable boundary conditions that can be geometrically interpreted as D-branes within specific theoretical models based on products of group- and coset-spaces, which are generalized versions of lambda deformations. Utilizing a sigma-model approach, we found that all the established conformal brane geometries in the context of products of WZW models satisfy the required boundary conditions, thereby maintaining their integrability across the renormalization group flow in our sigma-models. The identified brane geometries comprise traditional G-conjugacy classes, their twisted counterparts generated by permutation automorphisms (permutation branes), and more generalized permutations branes.

As tasks increasingly rely on computer execution, the demand for reliable solutions grows along with the necessity for accurately structured input. In problems requiring a mesh, hexahedral elements hold a preferred status, especially in tasks where the computation intensively relies on the local characteristics of the mesh, such as in the solution of partial differential equations and shape optimization. This document provides a standardized and efficient scanning and generating method for such meshes to support numerical applications and programming initiatives. An added hexahedral patch module in OpenScanner, combined with an algorithm for repairing "wild" nodes, enables accurate and efficient scanning and generation. Consequently, an OpenObjectDatabase containing only hexahedral elements can be used for a wide array of numerical computations, accompanied by an extended version of the OpenObjectDatabase class for precise input of mathematical functions.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting a new triple's correctness. Specifically, when a new
triple is generated, it's crucial to first identify the correct subject-object
relationship. Relation extraction, on the other hand, seeks to identify specific
kinds of relationships between objects within given text. We propose that these
two tasks are interdependent, and that relation extraction lays a solid
foundation for effective link prediction. Given this, we deviate from the norm
of utilizing pre-trained models in relation extraction and instead present GIN,
a lightweight model that performs well in both relation extraction and link
prediction tasks. Additionally, our multi-task approach improves the performance
of link prediction on the Wikidata dataset.

This study introduces an innovative analytical delay model specifically tailored for deep submicron CMOS inverters. Developed based on the critical recognition that inverter delay is a complex interplay of multiple process variables and load capacitance, the proposed model incorporates parameterized equations derived using least-squares minimization to accurately reflect this dynamic relationship. In comparison to simulation results generated by SPICE, the analytical delay model exhibits remarkably minimal error, averaging less than 2% for a wide range of technological parameters.

Making optimal decisions in complex, continuously changing environments requires
assuming certain conditions. Often, researchers assume a certain level of consistency
in the decision-making model known as the Q-function. However, in numerous real-world scenarios,
this condition does not hold true. Instead, we propose a more adaptable way of measuring the consistency
of Q-functions using statistical methods that work with samples. These methods can choose between
two different approaches, based either on how we measure consistency or how we measure deviation from it.
 Additionally, we demonstrate that our consistency measure meets expected requirements and can be used
to create a more stable form of function value convergence even in completely unpredictable situations.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by the quantity of shared components among different entities. In this study, we propose an alternative explanation, which integrates both possibilities through Bayesian statistics, suggesting that the presence of animacy is not only determined by the activation of specific animal-related areas but also by their variable engagement in overlapping neural circuits. This model, inspired by the idea that similar entities map to similar neural areas, can explain why the posterior inferior temporal area, Fulton, and Igor's studies observed gradual animacy gradients in single neurons. This gradient explains not only how animacy increases or decreases but also how different categories like living vs. non-living, man vs. woman, etc., are distinguished. This engagement-based engagement explanation offers a more nuanced understanding of how the ventral temporal cortex represents and distinguishes between various objects within the world.

In scientific simulation, achieving accurate replication of real-world scenarios is a top priority. However, commonly used methods such as the finite element method and finite volume method are often prone to inaccuracies and artifacts, including Gibbs oscillations, resulting in Gibbs artifacts that distort critical data like concentration profiles and temperature distributions. A novel approach presented in this research involves addressing these inaccuracies and artifacts by applying anisotropic smoothing to the data, a strategy that has been effectively applied in previous studies. By combining this technique with numerical simulations of oil spills, researchers have gained a deeper understanding of the looping currents and twisting motions that lead to the formation of loops, enabling the development of a predictive oil spill model. Moreover, the method can be adapted to accommodate a variety of boundary conditions, making it a versatile tool for a wide range of applications.

Quasi-periodic oscillations type C, typically observed in low-hard and hard-intermediate states of black hole X-ray transients, have been examined using the MAXI J1535-571 data collected by Insight-HXMT. By applying a novel time-dependent Comptonization model, observed evolution of Comptonization index and seed photon flux in these oscillations was explained. Observations suggest three frequency maxima in the 2-128 s range, each corresponding to different accretion jet states changes. These findings are consistent with measurements from quasi-periodic oscillations in other black hole transients.

In the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly for tasks requiring cooperation and communication, MARL agents are prone to being brittle due to their potential for overfitting on the policies of their training partners. As a result, they may adapt strategies centered on preconceived expectations of other agents' actions rather than truly reacting to their behaviors. To address this issue, we developed an innovative framework that utilizes self-interaction as a reactive mechanism for cooperative agents to facilitate improved adaptability and resilience in mixed teams. This framework utilizes the latent representations of agents' shared history to derive contextual information that enables agents to make decisions grounded in observed behaviors rather than assuming partners will follow predetermined policies. Through extensive evaluations involving multi-agent cooperative and competitive scenarios, our findings indicate that our agent design produces superior performance, particularly on diverse teams, by contrast to existing MARL approaches.

We introduce MatSim, a comprehensive synthetic dataset, benchmark, and 
approach designed to leverage computer vision for identifying and 
transferring similarities and transitions across materials and textures. 
MatSim enables one-shot learning, empowering the identification of any 
material regardless of the context or circumstances using only one or 
multiple examples. Visual material recognition is a crucial element in 
several industries such as food processing, agriculture, and industrial 
production. Our work involves leveraging vast resources commonly used 
by computer graphics artists to develop a CGI dataset centered around 
material similarity, incorporating physics-based rendering, varied 3D 
object assignments, and diverse environmental conditions to simulate 
real-world scenarios. To accommodate applications requiring a seamless 
transition between states, we simulate a gradual material transformation 
and also render materials within distinct contexts to facilitate a 
phenomenon-based approach. To accommodate a diverse range of use cases, 
we establish a tripartite evaluation metric assessing similarity, 
transitions, and diversity. Our experiments involve evaluating various 
existing models and developing a tailored Material-CNN architecture, 
which we also apply to a real-world scenario involving automatically 
identifying and describing used oil states from real-world images. Our 
goal is for MatSim to serve as a foundational point for future research 
and we encourage further development of computer vision capabilities 
for real-world applications.

Two equivalent formulations of Lie 2-algebras are recalled: one as a categorification of Lie algebras and another as a 2-category equivalent to the category of homotopy Lie algebras. Furthermore, we prove that all types of 2-categories, including those defined by a single map or multiple maps with specific properties, can be interpreted as Lie 2-algebras.

We introduce a novel method for local image feature matching, where instead of a sequential process, we first identify pixel-wise dense matches at a basic level and refine the good matches at a detailed level. In contrast to other dense methods, we leverage self and cross attention mechanisms in the Transformer model to derive feature descriptors that are context-dependent for both images. This approach allows our method, known as LoFTR, to effectively find dense matches in low-texture regions where traditional detectors face difficulties. Experiment results on indoor and outdoor datasets demonstrate that LoFTR surpasses current state-of-the-art methods with significant margin and excels on visual localization tasks, topping rankings on two prominent benchmarks.

The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, specifically in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, Bperp. This bias is identified as a systematic error in magnetic field measurements due to a particular degeneracy associated with the mixture of magnetic components. Statistical analysis reveals that a significant bias is present and affects a substantial portion of a large dataset from the SOLIS instrument. The magnitude of the bias is found to be around 10% of Bperp and correlates with the intensity of the magnetic field and the distance from the line-of-sight to the center of the magnetic field element. Two possible reasons for the bias are discussed, and further research is suggested to confirm the existence of the bias and its underlying causes.

This research paper explores a real-world scenario in which energy producers manipulate their power generation in response to varying electricity demands. A straightforward convex optimization technique is employed to identify the best secondary market price for each moment, with the goal of promoting energy efficiency during peak hours. System load predictions are used to create a step-climbing schedule for price adjustments, effectively enticing consumers to move their peak-time energy consumption to off-peak hours. The proposed approach is designed for real-time operation and can be integrated easily, with simulated results demonstrating its efficacy.

The generalized form of the Einstein theory, the Rastall theory of gravity, incorporates the law of conservation of energy and momentum. We derive a charged black string solution using the Newman-Janis approach in a Rastall theory background. Next, we investigate thermodynamic properties, such as Hawking temperature, for these black strings and study their graphical representations with respect to event horizons. Additionally, we examine the impact of Rastall theory on Hawking temperature and assess the charged black string stability. Furthermore, taking advantage of these black string strings, we investigate the possibility of mapping Rastall theory to quantum Rastall theory using the Hawking-Page transition.

The results demonstrate that the power-law decay rates found in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem for discrete systems directly correspond to pointwise scaling rates of a spectral measure with a spectral value of one. Moreover, assuming weak convergence, when no spectral gap is present, the convergence rates of the time-average in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem rely on sequences of infinite time as they tend to infinity.

The research on extremely old and metal-poor stars within our Galaxy is crucial for understanding its chemical development and the original star formation processes that shaped our cosmos. In the outer reaches of our Galaxy, a region called the Outer Halo stands out as an enigmatic area with few star clusters and a possible link to the Galaxy's formation. Studies on these outer regions have revealed both old, metal-poor stars and younger, more metal-rich populations. To gain insight into the history of this area, we searched for metal-poor stars in this region, using data from the Gaia survey to select candidates based on their parallax and motion, and then analyzing their motion within the Galaxy, and metal content through spectroscopic analysis, finding that some of these stars have unusual patterns in their motion within the Galaxy, and overall, the findings support the idea that the Outer Halo is a diverse area with multiple phases of development.

This research splits the Earth into a grid of hexagonal cells to collect and analyze worldwide data on daily fire counts from each cell to evaluate seasonal fire severity, defined as the total number of fires per season. A season is either spring or autumn, and lasts for two three-month periods. The analysis utilizes satellite imagery to determine fire counts, allowing for the identification of fire seasons worldwide. The findings reveal that the majority of regions on Earth experience autumn fire seasons of around three months or shorter. Furthermore, the study discovers that the length of fire seasons worldwide has not been increasing over the past twenty-one years, despite an overall growth in the total number of fires. The total number of fires worldwide has shown a significant increase over the past 21 years, but this growth is not uniform and can be influenced by various concurrent trends such as agriculture, economic, climate, and human population changes. The study investigates the influence of climate change, specifically atmospheric and oceanic temperature variations, using advanced multivariate time series analysis techniques, including nonlinear convolutions and trends removal, on both fire counts and fire severity over long and short periods. A significant correlation between temperature changes and fire severity trends was observed over the past 41 years, suggesting that global atmospheric temperature fluctuations significantly affect the number of fires over a large part of the Earth's surface.

We've conducted a thorough examination of eight distinct methods for evaluating the morphological intricacy of languages. These measures have different prerequisites for data annotation, yet our study identifies both similarities and disparities among them. We compare the methods visually and statistically. This visual analysis makes it possible to group the methods by similarity and to identify outliers. The statistical comparison confirms that some methods are significantly equivalent and also highlights clusters of related measures. The first principal component of the correlation matrix, for example, is primarily composed of components representing log-log scale and syllable count. This cluster includes MFC, FMC, and TMC. Our study also reveals that the complexity measures for Latin languages tend to cluster separately. This clustering might be attributed to the reduced variability in word lengths within these languages due to past cultural influences. Additionally, we found that the family affiliation of languages can impact the value of the morphological complexity measures. This effect is most pronounced for measures calculated from word frequency data. Our findings demonstrate that some complexity measures are significantly correlated, which might explain the overlapping results we previously observed between MFC, FMC, and TMC. Nevertheless, other measures, such as WMC and PCM, do not exhibit strong correlations with the other measures. Our study suggests that the establishment of a unified scale could facilitate the comparison of the various morphological complexity measures.

Researchers at Meneghetti et al have discovered an increased occurrence of small gravitational lens effects within galaxy clusters. To examine its impact, they compared self-interacting dark matter models with standard cold dark matter models, focusing on how dark matter interactions affect small-scale substructure within clusters. Using a strong lensing simulation tool, they found that self-interacting dark matter, which loses energy and becomes more concentrated, develops less dense substructures compared to standard cold dark matter. As a result, self-interacting dark matter, which loses energy faster, results in fewer and less massive substructures. These properties correlate with the characteristics of strong lensing effects, indicating a reduced occurrence of small-scale substructure lens effects in self-interacting dark matter models. To avoid conflicting with observations of satellite galaxies in galaxy clusters, any self-interacting dark matter scenario must occur at a lower magnitude than previously thought and typically requires additional baryonic interactions to strengthen the dark matter interactions. Future investigations of these substructures in both galaxy and galaxy cluster contexts are needed to shed light on the properties of dark matter.

This research focuses on reducing the complexity of parametric partial differential equations (PPDEs) by finding an accurate approximation space for the solutions of the equations. Given incomplete information, we use two primary sources: initial assumptions about the solutions and partial measurements from the equations. Based on these sources, we have developed methods to generate effective approximation subspaces and analyzed their performance. By identifying the optimal performance limit and providing simplified methods to achieve it, we have made strides in addressing the challenges associated with reducing the dimension of PPDE solutions while accounting for incomplete information about the equations or their solutions.

This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') approach ('m-ar-K-FastICA') for feature extraction, combining kernel-based dimensionality reduction with ICA to overcome the limitations of previous methods. Although the kernel trick offers a powerful way to tackle nonlinearity, its effectiveness can be undermined by a lack of open-source and reproducible kernel implementations, especially in complex datasets. The proposed m-ar-K-FastICA approach uses a readily available and adaptable Python library that facilitates collaboration with other techniques, such as deep learning. To validate the performance of m-ar-K-FastICA, the study compares it with established methods, including FastICA and k-means, on random data and a real-world dataset from the PhysioNet Challenge. In both cases, m-ar-K-FastICA exhibits significant advantages over the comparisons, with improved results obtained in both cases. The research shows that m-ar-K-FastICA can be an effective tool for feature extraction when working with complex or nonlinear data, including cases where dimensionality reduction is necessary but difficult. Additionally, the study highlights the importance of developing and implementing ICA using open-source and reproducible approaches, such as the m-ar-K-FastICA method.

Identifying trending social media events in real-time across various geographical locations is crucial, particularly for anticipating incidents such as accidents, protests, or breaking news. The dynamic nature of social media data poses challenges in creating a unified knowledge base, necessitating an adaptive framework that can incorporate and consolidate information from diverse sources. Our proposal, GeoEvent, is a real-time event detection system that utilizes social media data to identify and geotag events, and can be scaled up for massive data sets. It is effective in detecting emerging trends and is suitable for applications such as disaster response, consumer behavior analysis, and public opinion monitoring.

We establish the optimal Lipschitz regularity of very weak solutions for the measure-valued elliptic PDE $-\mathrm{div}(A(x) \nabla u) = Q \; \mathcal{H}^{n-1} \llcorner \Gamma$ within a smooth domain $\Omega$ of dimension $n$. Here, $\Gamma$ represents a $C^{1+\alpha}$-smooth hypersurface, with $Q$ denoting the surface density of a given Borel measure on $\Gamma$. Furthermore, the tensor field $A$ satisfies standard ellipticity and symmetry conditions. Given these assumptions, we prove that $u$ enjoys Lipschitz regularity throughout $\Omega$, with its Lipschitz constant dependent on the density $Q$ and the hypersurface $\Gamma$. This very weak form of regularity encompasses a broad scope of applications, including free boundary problems, volume-constrained interface problems, and singular perturbations. The key to this analysis lies in an improved version of the classical $C^{1,\alpha}$-regularity theory for elliptic PDEs, with the added feature of "measure source terms". The provided framework has been designed to be versatile, allowing its application to multiple equations that include nonlinear surface diffusion problems, modulated stability problems, and the peeling method's related results.

Advanced permanent magnets made from rare earth and transition metal alloys achieve high magnetization due to high transition metal content. By utilizing computational searches based on fundamental laws, researchers predicted 37 cobalt-rich compounds, specifically $M$Co$_{15}$, that exhibit rare-earth-free properties and a capacity to maintain stability at elevated temperatures. These compounds, each composed of two rare earth elements and cobalt, are evaluated as next-generation permanent magnets. Initial results indicate that $R$Co$_{15}$ has a stable crystal structure at high temperatures, yielding a rare earth element's Curie temperature. Moreover, these compounds may surpass current permanent magnets in terms of magnetization and resistance to magnetic field.

In the field of display advertising, real-time bidding has become the predominant approach. Each ad impression resulting from user interaction is instantly auctioned off, with demand-side platforms (DSPs) providing bids immediately following receiving auction request information from the publisher. The bidding process involves a trade-off between two conflicting interests - the desire to secure a high winning bid and the risk of incurring loss if the bid is excessive and results in a loss. The decision is further complicated by the uncertainty surrounding the value of an advertisement space at the time of bidding. This study examines how risk averseness influences bidding strategies in real-time bidding. We propose an optimal bidding strategy based on a fundamental principle of risk averseness, and demonstrate its effectiveness through theoretical analysis and numerical case studies. The results indicate that taking risk averseness into account when formulating a bidding strategy can yield a substantial increase in revenue - up to a 13% rise.

Nonclassical properties in continuous-variable quantum systems are often marked by quantum correlations and Wigner negativity. This study explores how these two nonclassical traits are connected in the context of remotely generating Wigner negativity in a passive quantum system controlled by two parties. Go-Simon criteria are applied to analyze when remote control can achieve Wigner negativity. Research demonstrates that quantum steering is a prerequisite for successful remote Wigner negativity. A specific example is provided using an two-modes squeezed vacuum state and two Mancini states, showcasing the diversity of scenarios in which Wigner negativity can be achieved remotely.

Accurate secure boundary analysis is crucial for practical quantum key distribution systems, but the current approach overlooks a critical aspect – the randomness consistency of seeds used in privacy amplification. We introduce and prove a quantum leftover hash lemma that applies to non-uniform random seeds, leveraging min-entropy, and then use it to establish a precise, error-corrected secure boundary for QKD systems that take into account the randomness reliability of the seeds. Compared to previous research, this new approach offers a more precise secure boundary, but also requires an additional computational cost. We conducted simulations of the main QKD protocols and found that the secure boundary tightening is significant in many real-world scenarios, but the impact can be minimal when the seeds' reliability is very high. Due to the need for specific details about the random number generator's properties, we hope that standard measurement methods for evaluating random number generators can be adopted, providing the essential parameters needed to establish the secure boundary of a QKD system.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space.

We'll examine the diffusion process described by the equation $u_t(t, x) =
\tfrac{1}{2}\{x u(t, x)\}_{xx} - \alpha \{x u(t, x)\}_{x}$ with $u(0, x)
\ge 0$ and $\alpha > 0$, which has an interpretation as the dynamics of a
closed population with birth and death rates that are proportional to the
population's size times the population's mean and standard deviation, as
derivated by Feller. This diffusion is the unique conservative weak solution to
the nonlinear transport equation $\partial_t u + u \partial_x u = \tfrac{1}{2}x
\partial_{xx} u + \alpha \partial_x u$ with $u(0, x) \ge 0$. We will derive
the stochastic differential equation that generates this diffusion and
demonstrate its one-to-one correspondence with the equation's conservative solutions
and the diffusion process it generates. Additionally, we will derive a similar
model of an open population and provide a diffusion representation of this
model as the weak solution to the nonlinear transport equation with $u(0, x) \ge
0$.

In this work, we explore diagrammatic methods in waveguide QED systems with a focus on systems where multiple photons interact. By using effective vertex functions, we efficiently model complex multi-photon scattering problems in systems with arbitrary photonic environments. Our methods are capable of handling challenging problems that pose significant computational difficulties using traditional approaches. Building on this framework, we develop a practical method to analyze multi-photon scattering in systems with complex spectral structures. Our findings are reinforced through various examples, including systems featuring multiple dispersion interactions and multiple two-level emitters, simplifying a complex problem that was previously difficult to solve analytically.

A potential way to study low-mass dark matter is by utilizing boosted dark matter interactions. The framework for light dark matter interactions involving no spin is relatively well-established, but the same cannot be said for spin-dependent interactions. The current work represents the first complete derivation of spin-dependent cross-section calculations for boosted dark matter interactions. Significant findings reveal that at higher boost velocities, the distribution of the proton structure matrix becomes non-uniform and an energy-dependent asymmetry appears, which needs to be considered for accurate cross-section calculations. The new interactions also result in novel process considerations such as forward-backward asymmetry and a matrix element that are absent in non-spin interactions. Consequently, the absence of rapidity dependence in some cross-section terms is observed during inelastic scattering processes. The influence of the proton structure matrix's time component on its distribution was also observed in this scenario, suggesting that at higher boost velocities the distribution becomes increasingly anisotropic.
This note employs Faulhaber's Formula to elucidate why odd Bernoulli numbers equate to zero.

Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of one symbol duration. Nevertheless, it experiences reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection methods. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By accounting for delayed trellis minimums in relation to delay periods, an increased set of rotating phases becomes possible, thereby expanding the solid angle angle and providing an improved level of resistance against receiver and transmitter phase shifts, Doppler shift, and symbol delay variations. It is observed that increasing the delay to 3 to 5 symbols yields an optimum level of resistance while still maintaining a comparable level of complexity and reduced bit error rates.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we have devised a novel technique that enables effective value estimates based on solitary ratings provided by humans. Our approach involves two interconnected training components: the first generates an optimal policy for a simulated environment without rewards, and the second utilizes this informed policy to make comparisons and uncover the environmental dynamics, leading to the creation of a reward function. Importantly, our method allows the learning environment to be defined by users through a structured interface, offering a high degree of adaptability and usability. Experimental results confirm the efficacy of our technique and validate your-grid world simulations with varying reward schemes.

We're exploring nucleon structure functions within noncommutative space-time, with the aim of uncovering the internal makeup of nucleons. To do this, we're utilizing corrected and novel vertices that arise from noncommutativity, and we're expressing the proton's structure functions using the noncommutative tensor \theta_{\mu\nu}. Our results are verified by comparing the calculated nucleon structure function (F_2(x)) to both experimental data and predictions from GRV, GJR, and CT10 models. Importantly, our structure functions align with GRV and GJR models but with an additional adjustment based on charm particles, as seen in CT10 predictions. Additionally, the proposed approach could have significant implications for noncommutativity in space-time theory.

In typical topological systems, significant disruptions trigger a phase shift, but we have developed an adjustable version of the Toric code that remains stable under even extreme external influences, characterized by a "critical line" where no phase shift occurs, and exhibits resilience against non-linear distortions. This outcome is due to the intricate interplay of frustration and non-linearity within the system, also enabling additional intriguing phenomena such as the reappearance of topological phases and the ability of topological order to withstand local measurement procedures. Our research paves the way for the creation of more reliable topological quantum codes that form the basis for large-scale quantum computing initiatives.

We investigate the eigenspectra of large, randomly constructed Hermitian block matrices, whose structure is perturbed by a finite rank complex modification. Given that the band's width expands faster than the square root of the matrix's size, our analysis demonstrates that the statistical distribution of the imaginary components of the eigenvectors aligns with the results from the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble. This finding was achieved using the methods and approaches developed in the arXiv paper, 1802.03813.

Recent advancements in dialogue tasks have been achieved through pre-trained language models. However, extracting meaningful dialogue context representations that can be utilized effectively remains a difficulty. Previous studies have explored the potential of Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) in capturing the underlying semantics of dialogue, but developing an AMR-based pre-trained model that can generalize well across datasets has proven elusive. This paper proposes a novel pre-training task that combines the ParaMap and ParaAMR datasets to build a semantic representation that encodes both meaning and part-of-speech information. The proposed model, ParaAMR-POS, outperforms baseline models and demonstrates superior performance in dialogue tasks, including dialogue classification, question answering, and response generation.

To establish trust and ensure fairness, as well as hold developers accountable, algorithmic interpretability must be measured. This study draws on principles from programming languages and learning theory to establish a comprehensive framework for assessing interpretability. This proposed method captures the essence of how a person learns an algorithm, and through rigorous evaluation, we prove its advantages in four key areas - it applies universally, can be computed easily, yields distinct results, and accurately tracks increasing complexity. By presenting the framework through a hypothetical scenario and elaborating its core concepts, we highlight the practical applications of this measurement tool, notably for those responsible for choosing between algorithms based on their merits.

Anomaly detection without labelled data is a highly challenging task that most machine learning models struggle with. In this paper, we develop an innovative weakly-supervised anomaly detection method that learns what is normal without needing manually labelled data. By using unsupervised mode propagation, we transform the anomaly detection problem into a classification problem where we train a deep neural network to identify normal data, then use its trained normal class to detect anomalies. Our proposed method harnesses the strength of fully supervised anomaly detection models like DeepHOLISTIC, which learns what is normal through propagation in a hidden space. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of our approach across a variety of visual anomaly detection datasets, outperforming other weakly-supervised and fully-supervised methods. Additionally, we showcase the applicability of our method in real-world anomaly detection applications.

A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. We introduce a novel approach to estimating the parameters of the Poisson process in a Bayesian framework, by transforming them using a tuning parameter'm'. This study develops a technique for selecting the optimal'm' value, which nearly orthogonalises the parameters, by minimising the correlation between their derivatives with respect to the parameters. By choosing this optimal'm', the parameters converge faster and efficiently in a high dimension. Furthermore, this method also enables asymptotic normality on extreme log-density estimates, which can be used as a normalising constant for extreme probability estimates by parameterization. We demonstrate that this approach leads to accurate estimates of extreme probabilities by performing simulations of maxima and real data analysis on both tail index and extreme probability estimates with multiple parameters. Finally, we apply this method to modelling extreme losses in transportation infrastructure.

This analysis addresses the challenge of optimizing cross-sectional area through a specific point within a geometric form. To generalize this concept, the approach is expanded across multiple dimensions. Nonetheless, the optimal average cross-sectional volume cannot be achieved at any arbitrary point; it can only be attained at the centroid of the shape. We then explore multiple scenarios where the average cross-sectional volume is maximized at the centroid, including cases with distinct geometric segments and uniform density distribution. Additionally, the average cross-sectional volume is maximized at the centroid in circular, elliptical, and rectangular geometries.

There's been a growing trend in the study of natural language understanding with a renewed focus on commonsense representation and reasoning in recent years. This resurgence has led to the creation of new commonsense knowledge graphs that can be used for set-wise reasoning, but there's still a lack of understanding about how to effectively represent and reason with this type of knowledge at a large scale. This paper argues that the problem lies in how we define and apply our goals, particularly in how we evaluate models, which often prioritizes exact matches over other forms of set-wise reasoning. This paper aims to change this by introducing a new task, multi-premise reasoning, which can provide more insights into how humans reason and make better choices for future model evaluation. By developing this new task, this paper creates a new benchmark by analyzing how humans reason and make better choices through multi-premise analysis and develops a new model that can effectively reason and make better choices based on two large, annotated datasets. This paper also argues and demonstrates that the quality of future CSKGs will be greatly improved if they are designed with multi-premise reasoning in mind.

We introduce the data processing pipeline developed for the Hi-GAL survey. This critical component is an integral part of the Herschel satellite project that's mapping the Galactic plane's inner regions. Leveraging a combination of Herschel Interactive Standard Environment capabilities and new, custom-designed tools, our pipeline effectively handles data reduction tasks. These include accurate data filtering, noise assessment, and efficient map generation that incorporate compactness to minimize artifacts. This process is fully automated and trustworthy through its use of clean and repeatedly verified code. We incorporate independent components to handle noise modeling and data analysis. We illustrate the pipeline's performance by examining its output in Hi-GAL Continuous Processng Initiative maps that cover the Galactic regions between -70 to -60 degrees in latitude. These observations, conducted at 240 micron with multiple scan speeds, demonstrate the significance of speed-dependent data processing in accurately capturing the Galactic plane's complex structures.

Recent photometric studies of the first population stars in multiple globular clusters have revealed varying iron abundances through horizontal branch morphological differences. Notably, [Fe/H] ratios correlated with stars' luminosity and color positions within these clusters' internal structures. Further investigation of surface iron values for red giants using the APOGEE-4 high-resolution spectrograph at the 2.7m Harlan J. Jennings telescope revealed new insights. Employing differential atmospheric models, our team obtained absolute iron values for $\eta$ Leonis Maioris, $\theta$ Boois, and M13, supplementing existing velocity data with these clusters' internal motions. Our findings showed diverse radial velocities and motions within these clusters and another, indicating possible multiple stellar generations and contributing to the understanding of varying horizontal branch morphologies and metal patterns within these globular clusters. These generated iron values could help address long-standing questions regarding these clusters' internal structures and external appearances. These generated iron values could help address long-standing questions regarding these clusters' internal structures and external appearances.

To facilitate a deeper understanding of one-dimensional physical systems, we consider a simplified single file model. We derive an analytical solution for the complete first exit time statistics of an overdamped single file with absorbing boundary conditions, after which we apply these findings to investigate the speed-accuracy relationship, examining how this property is influenced by the mean squared displacement and the entropic repulsive forces within the system.

Quantum Mechanics contradicts the universally assumed, classical cause-and-effect relationship established by Bayes' rule in physics. While believed to hold true in Laboratory Earth, this rule fails with quantum probabilities, rendering them unsuitable for making predictions about quantum events, despite being useful for analyzing data after an event has occurred. This paper explores the consequences of quantum causality and their potential to resolve several longstanding physics enigmas, including black holes, cosmology, and the nature of time. It also suggests that Quantum Mechanics may be considered a statistical theory, similar to Classical Mechanics, with the potential to establish a quantum counterpart to the classical relationship between mass and energy.

We initially report findings regarding corrections to system size for the state equation, trace anomaly, and speed of sound, using two specific theoretical frameworks: a model for massless scalar fields and another based on quenched QCD, both applying periodic boundary conditions. Additionally, we share ongoing results involving the application of Dirichlet boundary conditions to quenched QCD.

W. Braunen and D. Kahn have established a significant advancement in their ongoing research on the connections between the Ext-groups of the Steenrod algebra and the algebraic structure of $\pi_*^{S}\otimes\pi_*^{F}$. Their approach makes use of the algebraic transfer homomorphism, $t: \widetilde{Ext}^{s,t}_{F_p*A,0} \to \widette{Ext}^{s,t}_{S*a,0}$, to provide a 'transfer' of information. We first review the introduction and notation, then prove that the transformation is injective, followed by a discussion of its broader implications and potential extensions.

Astronomers observing far ultraviolet wavelengths from Earth's orbit have been hindered by a bright signal due to geocoronal hydrogen Lyman-alpha radiation. To address this challenge, scientists utilized a hydrogen absorption cell within the FUSE instrument's payload to filter out this interference. Although the cell was initially intended for use during lunar transit observations, researchers discovered it also effectively eliminated the geocoronal signal, making it useful for a broader range of observations. By combining the cell with a spatial mode exchange, researchers were able to achieve approximately 50% transmission of desired astronomical signals while blocking the geocoronal interference. To confirm the cell's efficacy, scientists re-analyzed a dataset of solar flare observations, correcting for the unblocked portion of the signal and validating the cell's functionality.

Optimal distributed controller design under communication limitations can be
complicated unless specific system characteristics are identified. We introduce a
class of systems with symmetrical graph properties, specifically, Graph
Symmetric Systems (GSSs), which are capable of being controlled with decentralized strategies.
By leveraging this system class, we develop a approach to design optimal
distributed controllers that adhere to communication constraints for GSSs.
Additionally, this methodology is applied to a linear system with bounded
inputs and results in a optimal distributed controller for the GSS system.
Moreover, it is shown that even though the system does not possess symmetrical
properties, it is possible to convert it into a GSS without losing optimality,
thus allowing the existence of optimal distributed controllers with reduced
communication constraints.

Image search algorithms that retrieve and identify copied images from large databases comprise two main components: a neural network that converts an image into a transformation-resistant vector, and a high-performance but imperfect search algorithm. This paper introduces active indexing to optimize the interplay between these components, reducing a representation's loss through subtle, imperceptible modifications to images before their release. Our modifications enhance the image's retrievability, with the image editor's effects evaluated through a human subjective study. Additionally, we employ strategies to minimize the editor's unwanted effects and utilize techniques such as lossy compression and non-linear transformation to reduce the necessary image alterations. Experimental results on Widgits, Cubi, and Oxford datasets demonstrate that active indexing significantly improves both accuracy and speed of image search, with the average precision of top 100 retrievals increasing by 33%, 28%, and 24% respectively.

This study confirms that physical layer-based authentication is achievable in
Gaussian noise environments, with the caveat that an all-knowing adversary cannot be
beated. An examination of a model comprising two transmitting sources and one
receiving device revealed that this model aligns with prior research findings. It also
involved identifying a specific, manageable level of eavesdropping effort that would
allow the sources to perform unforgeable transmission. In this model, a two-part
challenge involves decoding a random message from transmitting source 1 and
decoding a joint random message from both sources. These challenges are crucial for
preventing the adversary from making assumptions and generating counterfeit
messages. The measures of eavesdropping effort are motivated by the need to ensure
that the adversary does not begin by obtaining extensive knowledge of the random
messages. The model's complexity necessitates a numerical method for solving the
optimization problem at its core, with the support of this thesis providing the
relevant calculations. An comparison with an alternative model requiring the
adversary to begin by making an initial guess was also conducted, with the
supporting calculations provided in the appendix.

Reevaluating the "dispersionless transport regime" of Brownian particles in inclined periodic potentials, we found that after entering a running state under the influence of a constant force, these particles display typical diffusive behavior without experiencing unique transient dynamics as previously hypothesized. The flat section in the dispersion evolution graph can be entirely attributed to the particles' wide spatial distribution resulting from an earlier stage of superdiffusion. Using a velocity distribution model based on one-dimensional Brownian motion and accounting for the time when particles first cross the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang criterion, we precisely calculated this distribution's asymptotic square root displacement in two distinct regimes: superdiffusion and diffusion. Moreover, we confirmed that the superdiffusion coefficient is dependent on the spatial correlation length of the particle distribution and demonstrated that as this distribution becomes increasingly localized, the superdiffusion coefficient transitions into the standard diffusion coefficient.

This paper presents an adaptable, localized predictive technique that builds upon Jord\'a's (2005) model, expanding it to a non-linear, multi-agent framework. In contrast to conventional DSGE-style estimators, this method’s primary characteristic is that it estimates model parameters in a manner unaffected by assumptions regarding the responses of variables to disturbances. Furthermore, this technique is capable of identifying critical details of the model, such as how various agents react to stimuli and how various units within an organization interact, at minimal computational expense. Utilizing this method, we re-examine the issue of varying fiscal multipliers and offer evidence supporting the concept that the fiscal response to stimuli differs based on the current state of the economy. Additionally, we uncover fresh insights into the behaviors of loan and credit practices at individual banks, revealing significant temporal fluctuations.

We investigate the influence of the electromagnetic quantum vacuum on the angular momentum of a charge q moving in a uniform magnetic field. The orbital angular momentum generated is due to photons in the vacuum that emit an energy back to the charge in proportion to n^2, a greater increase than that of the -2n\hbar of a charge in a Landau level.

The primary goal of Fine-Grained Named Entity Typing (FG-NET) is to accurately classify various entity types, such as "Senator" and "Actor", by considering the context of each mention within a sentence. Traditional approaches to FG-NET often employ the Euclidean metric, which is inadequate for complex data, especially with a large number of distinct entity types. To address this limitation, we introduce an alternative representation based on hyperbolic space, where the distance between types can be better represented. Specifically, we use the Unified MKC model, which combines knowledge and distributional semantics, to project the context as points in hyperbical space, and then measure the distances between each mention's point and potential label points to predict the actual type. To support the proposed model, we developed a custom Python package for entity typing that leverages the Faiss library, and validated the effectiveness of the new approach on two benchmark datasets, achieving type 1-error reduction of 5.6% and 11.3% compared to the MKC baseline.

This paper establishes upper limits on the Hankel determinants for the $H_2(3)(f)$ and $H_2(4)(f)$ special types, specifically within the univalent function class and the $\mathcal{U}$ class defined by a specific condition involving functions that are analytic within the unit disk $\mathcal{D}$, where $\mathcal{U}_s(f)=\{f \in \mathcal{U}: \mathfrak{R} (f(z)/z)$ is strictly increasing on $(0,1]$ . Additionally, we investigate lower limits on the Hankel determinants for the $H_2(3)(f)$ and $H_2(4)(f)$ special types within the $\mathcal{U}$ class and find tight bounds for the first kind of Hankel determinants for the $\mathcal{U}_s(f)$ class where $f(z)=1+az+bz^2$.

Achieving efficient and sustainable operation in cloud data centers largely relies on load balancing, and virtualization enables this by using a proactive load balancing approach that prevents service disruption and ensures stability. Unlike the traditional post-migration approach which is complicated and may fail to meet desired load balance goals, our proposed Prepartition strategy effectively divides VM requests into manageable sub-requests and allocates necessary resources prior to migration, thus ensuring effective load distribution. In contrast to reactive migration, our technique ensures fine-grained resource allocation and predefined load balancing objectives. According to simulations using real-world data, our Prepartition scheduling (PrepartitionOff) yields a 10-30% improvement in performance compared to existing load balancing methods across various performance metrics such as response time, user dropout rate, resource utilization, and physical server usage.

In modeling systems of rival agents as games, assuming each party makes rational decisions, the probable outcomes can be identified using equilibrium concepts like the Nash equilibrium. In various real-world scenarios, factors like weather, traffic or fiscal policy, beyond the agents' control, can impact game dynamics. Often, the equilibrium observed doesn't align with the actual cost functions of the agents. This research proposes the use of Nash Fixed Point Networks, a class of neural networks, to predict game equilibria based on state inputs. NFPN models take into account not only the direct interactions between agents, but also external factors influencing the game. By embedding the Nash equilibrium conditions as loss functions for neural network training, the probabilistic nature of equilibria can be captured. This work further introduces techniques for assessing uncertainty in model predictions. Experimental results using both theoretical and real-world data indicate that neural networks trained with NFPT are effective at predicting game equilibria.

This study tackles the issue of assessing causal influences in cases where some variables involved in ensuring causal validity are incompletely known. For these situations, we develop tight limits on the causal influences by solving two intricate optimization problems. The derived limits prove to be sufficient, leading us to introduce an optimization technique, enabling dimensionality reduction that lets users choose between bias minimization and strict confidence in causal influence assessments. The proposed method's performance is substantiated through experiments conducted on real-world datasets, showcasing its value.

Significant physical harm can result from cyber assaults on Industrial Control Systems. Although in-person assessments can reveal vulnerable system components, they may not be effective against covert attacks that bypass detection during prolonged operations. We present a predictive real-time monitoring method in this study to identify whether a system's safety might be compromised by stealthy cyber assaults. Specifically, our approach adapts previous findings in reachability analysis for attack impact assessment and extends them to incorporate non-intrusive attacks. We also demonstrate its applicability to linear continuous-time systems with control constraints and show its practical utility in evaluating attack impact when protective measures are implemented.

A precise summary can be derived from lengthy written documents via deep learning models, but English language models often benefit from larger datasets and more advanced technology compared to its Indian counterparts. This research aimed to develop a summary retrieval model tailored for English documents in the resource-scarce language of Hindi. Since a vast amount of labeled data is absent for this language, this study introduced a data augmentation approach to create a mock label based on the performance of a proxy model, which was also a low-resource language model. Furthermore, this paper suggested using a strong and pre-trained English model as a starting point for a cross-lingual Hindi summarization task. Firstly, pseudo labels were generated for an English proxy model from a mock label using the data augmentation approach. Then, this proxy model was trained on both pseudo and true labels to improve its performance. Following this, the this paper adapted an English BERT model for use in a low-resource Hindi summarization task. To accomplish this, this study used concepts from cross-lingual word embeddings and proposed a method of translating Hindi documents into an English space. Once the Hindi BERT model was created, this paper used true labels to fine-tune its English BERT model for use in a low-resource Hindi summarization task. Ultimately, this paper showcased the effectiveness of our data augmentation approach to create a mock label based on the performance of a weak and low-resource language model, which can be used as a starting point for a cross-lingual Hindi summarization task

We establish the definition and certain attributes of S-rings of Krull type, in addition to examining the properties of such structures, particularly independent S-rings of type A. We calculate the injective dimension of a quotient category formed by modules over an independent S-ring of type A, with respect to a specified subcategory consisting of modules having trivial interactions with codivisorial modules.

The objective of this research was to identify and characterise potential substellar companions associated with five rapidly accelerating stars using data obtained through adaptive optics imaging, radial velocity measurements, and constraints derived from astrometry. Spinning neutron stars are often surrounded by dense, boundary layers, and in some cases, a companion substellar object may be present. We looked at the astrometric data for the targets HIP 1481, HIP 28389, HIP 63442, HIP 78365, and HIP 88399 to see if any of these had orbital masses consistent with neutron star companions. Although the data for HIP 1481 and HIP 88399 suggested the presence of a substellar object, the data for the other targets did not provide any significant results. For HIP 1481 and HIP 88399, we were able to estimate the masses and radii of the potential companions, with model masses ranging from 10 to 60 Jupiter masses and radii ranging from 2 to 4 Jupiter radii. However, these models did not rule out the possibility of a rocky planet or a brown dwarf, so further observations are needed to confirm the presence and nature of these potential companions.

Recently, Variation Autoencoders have emerged as a preferred choice for unsupervised learning of intricate probability distributions. Compared to traditional autoencoders, VAEs exhibit enhanced reconstructive capabilities, making more accurate approximations possible even in the presence of noise, as opposed to Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. By utilizing a hierarchical series of probabilistic layers, VAEs formulate a generative process that involves an inference network used to find the most likely latent distribution given a given data point. We will explore the application of VAEs in generating prior distributions for Bayesian inference in neural networks, drawing parallels with Variational Inference and Approximate Bayesian Computation, while also discussing the challenges and limitations of this approach.

Smart home technology is gaining momentum, driven by IoT, yet it also invites cyber threats that necessitate robust and cost-effective security measures. This research contributes to filling this need by designing an affordable, network security system utilizing a private blockchain and a location tracking technique based on wireless signal strength. Our investigation highlights the benefits of private blockchains and optimizes the location tracking accuracy by testing its performance with various wireless networks. The results demonstrate that integrating a private blockchain with Wi-Fi technology achieves the best results for our proposed system.

A novel approach to quantizing log-likelihood ratio storage utilizing deep learning is presented. It was discovered that average L-values of QAM symbols consistently adhere to an ordered relationship, which facilitated the design of a deep autoencoder. By employing this autoencoder to pre-process L-values, a significant reduction in memory usage is achieved. The findings demonstrate that using 6 bits instead of 10 bits in L-value storage, while retaining over 99% of original information, is feasible. Moreover, this method can be generalized for use with any type of communication modulator.

We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs. Notably, this study presents the first parameterized algorithm with respect to vertex parameters for upward planar drawings. We expect these new algorithms to facilitate further applications in parameterized complexity, particularly in the realm of directed acyclic graphs.

Crowdsourced image datasets, often marred by noise, pose a significant challenge for even the most sophisticated neural networks. This difficulty arises from class imbalance and uncertainties in labeling, issues that are particularly prevalent in datasets consisting of images of ancient Greek papyri such as AL-ALL and AL-PUB, where individual characters are closely cropped from these images. The application of neural networks on these datasets resulted in substantial overfitting due to the prevalence of noise. To mitigate this problem, the ensemble approach was utilized by training multiple models with different regularization techniques, including dropout, batch normalization, and weight regularization, utilizing mock positive and negative samples with supplementary unlabelled data via active learning based on uncertainty measurements. The ensemble model, comprised of three CNNs, demonstrated the highest accuracy and reduced margin of error when compared to alternative models using precision, recall, F1-score, and Cohen's kappa metrics.

For semiflows with uniformly or nonuniformly expanding dynamics, which exhibit exponential decay in correlations, we can prove the exponential decay in the H\"older norm of the transfer operators acting on smooth observables.

Traditionally, constructing these grids with's' elements in each row, having a total of 'n' rows, and satisfying the 't' and 'q' condition, has been the focus - essentially, achieving a level of 't'-uniformity. A significant aspect of these grids is that their 'n' value must be a multiple of the least possible 't' 'q' value.
